We designed and built a rapid gamma-ray burst (GRB) simulator utilizing an electrical equivalent of the Suzaku MAXI detector. The device, capable of producing bursts at a rate of one per second, features a time-jitter measurement of 24.1 us and an energy resolution of 0.87 KeV at 6 KeV. This paper presents the development of the simulator and associated time-resolved calibration of the MAXI detector.

Let $T_g$ denote the integral operator defined by $T_g(f)(z) = \int_{\mathbb{D}} \frac{g(z+w)}{(1+zw)^2}dA(w)$ for $g \in BMOA_p$, $1 < p \leq 2$. This paper investigates the compactness of $T_g$ and establishes that it is equivalent to the compactness of the operator $S$, which is generated by compact functions in the space $BMOA_p$. Furthermore, this paper examines the relationship between $T_g$ and the subspace $BMOA_p^{\delta}$ for $\delta > \frac{1}{p'}$ and determines the optimal value of $\delta$ such that the compactness of $T_g$ is guaranteed when $g \in BMOA_p^{\delta}$. This optimal value is found to be the smallest solution to the equation $\frac{1}{p} + \frac{\delta}{1-\delta} = 1$.

The vast amount of knowledge published in scientific literature makes it difficult to track the evolution of knowledge over time. To address this challenge, we propose a method for quantifying the index of quantitative knowledge (KQI) to measure the spread of knowledge through time and across different fields. We use bibliometric data from 18 fields and observe how knowledge has increased over the past century, with the rate of knowledge growth accelerating in recent decades. Our results indicate that knowledge has become more dispersed, with a greater degree of differentiation occurring in the 20th century. We also discovered that the majority of knowledge originates from a small subset of highly productive authors, but our data suggests a more significant degree of author overlap than previously estimated. Furthermore, we found that knowledge has become more concentrated within a small subset of highly productive journals, with a greater degree of journal overlap appearing in the 20th century. Our analysis also revealed that knowledge has accelerated over the past century, with the degree of knowledge differentiation increasing in recent decades. We offer possible explanations for these trends, including the accelerating growth of the global economy and the rising demand for scientific knowledge.

A key challenge in wireless communication systems is providing both fast and secure data transmission. This concept is known as Fast Secure Transmission. We introduce an innovative power allocation strategy called Stackelberg Pre-Game Power Allocation. This method allocates power to different nodes in the transmission path with varying degrees of secrecy sensitivity, aiming to achieve Fast Secure Transmission efficiently. We demonstrate that our proposed approach consistently yields optimal security performance and can be implemented through a linear program. Additionally, we introduce an intuitive heuristic busting strategy that produces high-quality security results in a shorter timeframe. We verify the effectiveness of our methods through numerical experiments conducted on various complex systems.

Quantum emitters coupled to photonic platforms can facilitate the coherent exchange of information between spatially distant points, capitalizing on the unique properties of topologically-protected edge modes. It is proposed that emitters placed at critical points can be manipulated to create a non-local, entangled state between two regions defined by a photonic topological device. This state is safeguarded against local errors due to its topological nature, providing a foundation for the development of fault-tolerant quantum logic gates. A possible implementation of this concept is explored in a photonic box-like structure, with a photonic diode serving as an example of a non-local unitary operation. Coherent manipulation of a quantum emitter in this setup has been demonstrated using a superconducting quantum circuit, offering a viable path to realizing this vision technologically.

If an automated vehicle is approaching an intersection and is connected to the traffic signals, it can plan its path according to the remaining yellow and red signal phases through calculation of its speed. This paper explores the idea of automated vehicles calculating their optimal path based on their maximum acceleration and braking capabilities, and establishes a mathematical formula for this optimization. By analyzing the optimal path's curvature and determining its minimum value, this paper also proves that the optimal path corresponds to a straight line when traffic signals are fully considered. This finding is validated through simulation in various scenarios, including different traffic signal phases, vehicle acceleration and braking capabilities, and intersection geometry.

We introduce TextWorldExpress, a new toolkit for text-based game simulations, built on top of PyTorch and Pygame libraries. TextWorldExpress significantly boosts simulation speed, reducing the slow-down from running simulations in Python to nearly negligible levels. Our results show that TextWorldExpress achieves comparable performance to the original TextWorld, with only a minor decrease in accuracy. Additionally, TextWorldExpress demonstrates the ability to learn highly efficient policies on complex TextWorld tasks, outperforming previous benchmarks by a significant margin in compact actions mode. With TextWorldExpress, we establish new evaluation standards and benchmark scripts, making it easier for future researchers to compare their approaches with our top-performing models. Our code, models, and benchmark scripts are available for download at https://github.com/prajjuvaa/TextWorldExpress.

Deep learning techniques have rapidly matured in recent years but outdated model-based design strategies and limited on-chip memory have prevented further breakthroughs in deep neural network implementations. In this work, a novel architecture called FDHT-LSTM is developed, reducing both memory access patterns and required on-chip memory by two dimensions. Unlike traditional tensor decomposed model-oriented hardware, the new architecture achieves superior performance, outperforming the best existing HT and FT-based HT-LSTM implementations by 1.75 and 2 times in throughput and 2 and 3 times in energy efficiency, respectively. Furthermore, the on-chip memory usage is cut in half, enabling the successful batched evaluation of the largest LSTM matrix up to 64 times. The FDHT-LSTM architecture is designed with a flexible and reusable framework that allows easy extension to other deep learning algorithms, such as CNN and RNN. In addition, the amount of necessary off-chip data is significantly decreased by a factor of four, resulting in reduced data bandwidth usage. The FDHT-LSTM architecture is fabricated in a 16nm FinFET process with a 0.32mm silicon area, comprising 108k gates.

Recent advancements in NLP have shown that subtle, controlled perturbations in data can significantly boost model performance and improve model robustness. Nonetheless, comprehensive studies on NLP efficiency-enhancing data augmentation remain limited. We undertake an exhaustive investigation, encompassing 10 + NLP tasks across eight categories. Within each task, we explore diverse data augmentation techniques, including token-level, sentence-level, and batch-level manipulations. Our findings reveal that tailored data augmentation strategies lead to notable improvements, with improvements ranging from 1.25 to 11.38 in cone score. Our study also highlights that certain data augmentation methods, although often robust to changes in hyperparameters, can sometimes exhibit surprising sensitivity to them. Moreover, we observe that data augmentation efficiency correlates with the diversity of representations within the model, as indicated by a factor that reflects the second moment of embedding vectors. Our work lays the groundwork for future studies in NLP efficiency enhancement and offers straightforward implementations of data augmentation strategies on popular GitHub repositories.

A working version of the Weak Gravity Conjecture is proposed, involving a self-binding criterion that takes into account the impact of an external gravitational field on an existing weak gravity configuration. This concept is particularly relevant in flat space, where it is shown that a weak gravity state with charge $q$ and mass $m$ can be modified by an external gravitational field to change its properties to those of a state with charge $q'$ and mass $m'$, as long as $q \ll q'$ and $m \ll m'$. It is also demonstrated that in anti-de Sitter space, the self-binding criterion defines the ground state of a system consisting of a graviton and a graviphoton field. Additionally, it is argued that the cosmological constant $\Lambda$ can be viewed as a self-binding effect of a state with charge $q$ and mass $m$, resulting in the relationship $\Lambda \ll (q^2 + m^2)^2$, which has implications for the validity of the Weak Gravity Conjecture in relation to string theory on Calabi-Yau manifolds.

By developing a new quantum simulation model that incorporates an ensemble of multiple Hartree-Fock (MHF) wavefunctions, our approach significantly expands upon the traditional single-HF model. This enhanced model utilizes a range of realistic MHF states to simulate multiple simultaneous quantum states and their variations within an atomic or molecular system. Thanks to the linearized strong response method, Fock-space diagrams can be efficiently handled, making our MHF model a valuable tool for post-HF calculations. Additionally, our model adapts the time-dependent generalization of response theory to simulate time-dependent external fields and multi-photon responses. Incorporating an ensemble of MHF wavefunctions enables a more precise simulation of diverse quantum states, and our method offers an adjustable mixture of different quantum states. Notably, our model can naturally reproduce the exclusion of certain quantum states that cannot satisfy Pauli constraints, and it offers a more comprehensive description of electronic dynamics than single-HF theory. Several examples demonstrate the efficacy of our MHF response theory, including simulations of multi-photon responses, field-free and non-equilibrium phenomena driven by external fields, and the variation of quantum state mixtures in atomic systems.

Given a local ring R with an idempotent element $\mathfrak{f}$, we examine the zero submodule of the local cohomology module $\mathbf{H}^i_{\mathfrak{m}}(R,\mathfrak{f})$ for integer $i$. This investigation yields results that enable us to characterize the $F$-rationality of R and its associated prime ideals in the case of equidimensional rings. Additionally, we establish connections between the Milnor class group of R and the zero submodules of its local cohomology modules. These findings expand upon and refine previous research by Rui, Sharp, and Yousuke.

A growing interest in designing competitive wholesale electricity markets through mathematical modeling is an response to the complex issues faced by these markets. The case study presented here focuses on the redispatch market, exploring how it can be optimized through an all-or-none order design. This design allows generators to choose whether or not to participate in a generation reduction or increase opportunity, with the goal of minimizing costs. The optimization problem is defined and its structural properties are explored, and a numerical study is conducted to examine its results. The findings show that the optimal solution involves paying the most for the most expensive and least valuable redispatch options, and that the all-or-none design can effectively allocate value compared to a pay-per-megawatt-hour approach.

This paper builds upon a prior findings regarding Galois groups in function fields and polynomial analogues of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, specifically the result that a significant proportion of polynomials in a given field, with a specific degree and within a defined parameter, have a specific Galois group. The paper then explores this concept within the context of the polynomial analogue of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, confirming that a substantial proportion of polynomials, with a specific degree and within a defined parameter, are irreducible over the integers with a specific Galois group, i.e., a group that does not simplify to a smaller group when split into its constituent parts.

To evaluate the reliability of theoretical predictions for future Higgs boson experiments at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC), this study explores the accuracy of implementing practical production and detection processes within theoretical models. Specifically, the analysis examines the impact of producing pairs of top quarks on theoretical predictions for Higgs boson signals, assuming that top quark pairs can be accurately measured with high precision. The accuracy of theoretical predictions for Higgs boson signals can be significant, at 10^-3 or lower, largely depending on the specific process and theoretical model used. The findings suggest that it is necessary to consider the effects of producing pairs of top quarks on theoretical predictions for Higgs boson signals in order to make informed decisions about the design of future LHC experiments.

To explore the physics potential of the future precision studies at the ILC, specifically to test extended scalar sectors, this study investigates the sensitivity of measuring the Higgsstrahlung cross-section and the Higgs diphoton decay rate. If the Higgs boson decays to a dark photon instead of two photons, the corresponding Higgsstrahlleur process would offer cross-section measurements highly correlated with the diphoton decay rate. As a result, even if the dark photon decay mode is not directly detected with diphoton recoils, the measurement of the Higgsstrahlleur process would still place a corresponding lower limit on the decay rate. Consequently, the ILC can tightly constrain extended scalar sectors, such as a dark photon with an order-of-magnitude larger coupling than the standard model, which would be beyond the reach of precision studies at the LHC in its planned or semi-planned form.

Despite being a planet with very strong winds, Saturn's north polar stratospheric vortex (NPV) has been difficult to study using data from the Saturn orbiters, but recent analysis of data from the Saturn orbiters reveals their complete stratospheric and mesospheric view.  Using this data, researchers were able to study NPV and its surrounding polar jet for the first time and their analysis showed that NPV was stable and long-lasting, extending far into the summer months, unlike the Saturn polar stratospheric features observed during summer, which are temporary and break apart as quickly as they form.  Additionally, NPV was found to be surrounded by a steady west-to-east wind, known as the jet stream, which is a hallmark of polar jet streams and also remained consistent throughout the summer.  In addition to these features, researchers also observed a peculiar wave-like pattern of winds, known as planetary waves, that reached the Saturn north pole and shifted direction, changing from west-to-east to east-to-west winds, a phenomenon that has only been observed previously close to the Earth and Saturn's south pole.  Furthermore, the data showed that the NPV and its surrounding jet stream played a crucial role in shielding the planet's atmosphere from the solar wind and reduced the amount of charged particles entering the planet's interior, a finding that could have implications for the operation of satellite electronics within the Saturn system.

For a solution $u$ of the exterior boundary value problem for the Schrödinger equation given by $i\partial_t u=-\Delta u$ in $\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus B(0,R)$ with data $(u(0),\partial_t u(0))$ in the Sobolev space $H^1(\mathbb{R}^3 \setminus B(0,R))$, if the initial energy is sufficiently large, we demonstrate that the solution $u$ experiences blow-up both for the full space case and when confined to an asymptotically flat exterior domain. Our approach builds upon classical methods of proving blow-up by establishing a uniform estimate for the energy of solutions $u$ and provides a new approach to blow-up proofs, applicable to various types of nonlinear wave and dispersive equations, including the Schrödinger equation, Klein-Gordon equation, and surface wave equations.

This briefing note addresses the question of whether the category of finite-length modules over a commutative algebra in positive characteristic resembles the category of finite-length modules over the same commutative algebra in characteristic zero, given the assumption that the commutative algebra has an evident connection to a coherent sheaf on a coherent surface, essentially mapping to the ring of a coherent surface in characteristic zero.

We have demonstrated that the spectral weight'sum rules' no longer hold in highly correlated systems undergoing a metal-insulator transition, no matter the nature of the transition. This breakdown is reflected in the distribution of spectral weight across all energy levels and demonstrates that the metal-insulator transition involves a continuous spectrum change. Our findings are based on simulations of the Su-Schrieffer-Heeger model with periodic boundaries and coupled pairs, and we have verified that the spectral weight sum rules are an exception in highly correlated systems.

We investigate the dynamics of atoms in a quantum guide after a quantum double dark-soliton state is created through a quantum double dark-soliton initial condition. By applying quantum hydrodynamics theory, we are able to obtain an exact description of the quantum double dark-soliton state and its time-evolved form. Our analysis reveals how the density profile changes over time and identifies distinct phases of motion associated with quantum effects, including the formation of a quantum cavity and the propagation of a quantum soliton tail. The accuracy of our theoretical model is verified through comparison with experimental data and a 6D quantum simulation.

This research paper delves into the worlds of symplectic double vector bundles and symmetric k-fold vector bundles, establishing a direct relationship between them, thereby extending the fundamental connection found between them in "The Cartan Marchand-Saint-Raymond voice from the string theory perspective". We successfully map any symplectic double vector bundle to a symmetric vector bundle of order k, for any positive integer k, and demonstrate the reversibility of this process. Furthermore, this correspondence yields distinct achievements: it creatively employs the natural symplectomorphism to define the symmetric vector bundle, and it establishes the equivalence relation that defines the symmetric k-fold vector bundle through the natural projection of the symplectic double vector bundle.

For the Lie algebra $A_n$, we establish relationships between Kirillov's measure, geometric measure on orbits, and the dual variable measure, expressing them in terms of each other and the Euler vector field. Additionally, we demonstrate the compatibility of these measures with the highest weight corresponding to the fundamental weights.

A recent algorithm has been introduced that accelerates the deconvolution of x-ray scattering spectra using the Fourier p-slice method, and this talk will demonstrate its application in this context. Initially developed to solve phase retrieval problems employing the Fourier p-slice method, the new algorithm speeds up the deconvolution process for x-ray scattering data in comparison to the traditional approach. To validate its effectiveness, the algorithm was tested on synthetic data and in experiments utilizing the MAXII storage ring at the Lund University's high-energy storage ring and the European Synchrotron Radiation Facility WA108 beamline. The results show that the new algorithm achieves comparable accuracy while significantly reducing the time required for calculations. This improvement is particularly beneficial for data analysis at high-energy facilities.

We invite researchers to participate in an ongoing discussion about the interconnections between classical disordered statistical mechanics and quantum error correcting codes. A series of quantum code variants, each drawing from classical counterparts like random bond Ising, Sherrington-Kirkpatrick, and Edwards-Anderson models, are displayed through exact and sampled solutions of their respective partition functions. These representations showcase the dual nature of these quantum systems, where both their classical and quantum aspects converge to analogous limits. Furthermore, we highlight potential future research directions that could bridge the gap between these quantum ensembles and real-world experiments and simulations.

To break through the limitation of small non-trivial gaps in quantum well structures, research focus has shifted to non-symmetric quantum well designs. However, quantum well structures face a significant obstacle in realizing a notable non-trivial gap under external bias due to their inherently small gap sizes. We propose using strain engineering to enhance the non-trivial gap in Tellurene-based quantum well structures, showcasing that a significant gap increase can be achieved in both asymmetric and symmetric well designs. Our analysis reveals that the larger non-trivial gap in these structures arises from the modified electron and hole profiles in both the well and barrier regions, which are a result of applying strain. Moreover, we find that this gap enlargement is strain-direction dependent and can be adjusted by modifying the strain orientation. Our study also highlights the potential of Tellurene-based quantum well structures to serve as reliable devices for logic operations in the quantum computing industry.

To account for blocking fractures, we modify the standard Darcy flow model by introducing a non-conforming finite element method using the Mortise and Pilon function approach for double layer potentials. We investigate how the Mortise and Pilon approach relates to the Dirac-beta function approach and examine its asymptotic behavior as the Mortise and Pilon parameter approaches zero or infinity. We derive an error bound for the non-conforming finite element method in terms of an energy norm and observe that this error bound reflects the impact of this parameter on the error, indicating potential improvements as it approaches zero or infinity. However, we note that when this parameter approaches zero or infinity, the corresponding impact on blocking fractures becomes less significant, ultimately leading to a potential decrease in this term's magnitude.

The spin-valve behavior of lateral nanocontacts made from ferromagnetic materials and carbon nanotubes exhibits an interesting phenomenon when subjected to exchange fields of moderate strength. Despite expectations that the spin-valve effect would diminish significantly, our experiments reveal a notable increase in the spin-valve effect at exchange fields of approximately 10 kOe. The application of an external magnetic field to one of the spin-valve layers causes the spin polarization to shift notably, leading to a greater difference in resistance between the parallel and anti-parallel configurations. This phenomenon arises due to a shift in the population of spin subbands under the influence of the exchange field, which results in a change in the conductance of the nanocontact in a particular way. A simple theoretical model has been developed to understand this behavior, predicting that the largest gain in the spin-valve effect would occur at exchange fields corresponding to the splitting of heavy and light effective mass subbands.

The H0 validation problem is a challenge in statistical analysis where a well-established null hypothesis, often incorporated into a modeling framework, is difficult to disprove due to its vast parameter space. To address this challenge, a Bayesian approach has been developed that prioritizes null hypothesis validity by assigning a utility function to evaluate the outcomes of model-based inferences. This approach enables the systematic selection of the best model based on its ability to validate the null hypothesis, and has been successfully applied in the context of Gaussian graphical models. Building on this work, the approach has been expanded to accommodate a broader class of graphical models characterized by their sparse and Markov random field properties. A suite of efficient computational tools has been developed to support this extension, including an efficient sampler for the model space and a utility function evaluator that leverages the principles of Monte Carlo approximation. Collective efforts have yielded a robust algorithm capable of handling substantial data sets.

Our newly created dataset DiscSense is the first large-scale, annotated collection relating discourse markers and semantic relations in modern Arabic. This dataset consists of 6340 sentence pairs, spanning across four categories of discourse markers, and is supplemented by a concise guide to discourse markers in Arabic. To ensure the reliability and practical usability of DiscSense, we developed a series of experiments utilizing both supervised learning models and automatic evaluation tools. These experiments demonstrate the utility of DiscSense in both modeling the relationships between words within sentences and the connections between sentences, as well as the potential for further research in these areas. Additionally, DiscSense offers a valuable educational tool for learners of Arabic discourse through its annotated guidelines.

For years, researchers have been attempting to grasp the mechanics behind the rapid decay of excited states in transition metal oxides, yet a comprehensive theory has yet to be developed. A recent proposal, based on principles from the Mott-Seitz model and the Zener theory of charge transfer, seeks to provide a unified explanation for the high-energy cost of nonradiative decay through its connection to the bandgap structure. Using this framework, a proposed $O^{2-}$ to $O^{2-}$ charge transfer energy is calculated to be $6.5\pm0.5$ eV for all perovskite materials, matching the outcome of more precise calculations based on the Fano antiresonance theory. This model also predicts that the width of the upper Hubbard band should be around $1\pm0.5$ eV, which can be verified through experimental measurement. Finally, it is suggested that the frequency of the local phonons matching the energy of the upper Hubbard band should be in the range of $30\pm10$ meV.

We introduce an innovative neural network training technique that diverges from backpropagation's reliance on error gradients. Instead, our method computes the derivative of a objective function in relation to network inputs and weights, utilizing local linearizations and quadratic proxies. The algorithm's efficacy is demonstrated through its application to supervised learning tasks, resulting in similar performance but with reduced training time. Furthermore, our technique facilitates neural network design by enabling efficient exploration of multiple training trajectories, thus allowing for the creation of robust models. We validate our findings with experiments involving fully connected networks, convolutional neural networks, and recurrent neural networks.

We investigate a $3d$  Abelian gauge model with a nontrivial target space, which leads to the presence of magnetic skyrmions and monopoles in $3d$ and $4d$ dimensions, respectively. The dynamics of these objects are determined and their interactions analyzed. The homotopy group of the target space defines the variety of magnetic skyrmions, with example rotations being identified. The gyration frequencies of these skyrmions increase with spin number, with a corresponding scaling of the skyrmion size. We find that skyrmion sizes are sensitive to the nontrivial target space component when this varies significantly, with potential experimental implications. The gyration frequencies of monopoles also scale with the spin number when the nontrivial component is small, with frequencies potentially accessible by experimentalists. The interactions between these objects with different spin numbers result in complex scenarios, with waves on a surface potentially harboring multiple skyrmions. The theoretical framework can be applied to pions, with the result that skyrmion sizes are similar to those found in other gauge models, with sizes potentially as small as a few hundred km.

We investigate how the magnitude of electron-electron Coulomb interaction affects the convergence of the Hartree-Fock method when using local correlation functions as the basis. Our analysis utilizes the atomic hydrogen as a test case and demonstrates that a simple modification of the Hartree-Fock equations can facilitate rapid convergence across various states of motion, especially in intermediate energy regions. This improvement in convergence is found to be highly robust and is further explored in relation to the density of states and energy convergence for both ground and excited states.

In complex networks, the coexistence of dynamic and structural disorders within network nodes leads to an increasingly sophisticated scenario. Despite the growing interest in this field, the absence of an exhaustive theoretical framework hinders our understanding of highly inhomogeneous networks. Utilizing a coupled map lattice to analyze this type of network, our study reveals that explosive synchronization can result from an abrupt transition within a narrow range of inner connectivity values, even in networks of fully non-linear nodes. Our findings indicate that subtle variations in network structure can give rise to distinct polarized dynamics, while also exhibiting robustness in the face of network reconfigurations. Our analysis highlights the significance of distinguishing between hysteresis and memory effects in empirical observations, as well as the potential for over- or under-estimation of activation states. Ultimately, our research demonstrates that intricate dynamics within highly inhomogeneous networks are characterized by multi-stable polarization states, capable of displaying explosive synchronization phenomena as a result of a subtle, first-order transition.

We explore how a specific optimization problem with a matrix variable can be broken down into easier sub-problems that factorize the variable. This will be done under certain conditions and within a specific geometric framework, and our goal is to identify when the optimized factorized function exhibits similar geometric properties to the original optimized function. Our approach results in a precise error bound for an average-based iterative algorithm used to solve this problem. Our findings are relevant to various big-data applications and can be applied to optimization methods that rely on random sampling.

In 1990, Yang and Yang proposed a conjecture that a bipartite graph with maximum degree 3 can be colored using a strong edge-coloring with an alternating pattern if it has at least $k$ components, where $k\geq5$ when the degree is 3 and $k\geq2$ when the degree is 2. This study aims to verify the conjecture's first part for graphs with the maximum degree 3.

The purpose of this paper is to provide explicit identities that connect Gauss sums to the square values of certain Dirichlet $L$-functions at $s=2$. Additionally, we derive an identity for Dirichlet $L$-functions in the form of $L(p^2,2)=\frac{1}{2}(\frac{\pi}{N})^{\frac{2}{2}}S_{2}(p)$, where $S_{2}(p)$ is expressible through Gauss sums.

Researchers anticipate finding a background signal from gravitational waves generated during the early universe's primordial era. However, if heavy particles were present at the universe's birth, they would have produced gravitational waves quickly, leaving no observable trace. Additionally, such particles might also affect the sound of gravitational waves emitted during cosmic inflation. Using a new approach to reevaluate existing data, scientists have found that if heavy particles existed just beyond the current detection limit, they could potentially eliminate the evidence for background signals in future inflationary sound measurements. As a result, researchers suggest that heavy particles' existence be considered when interpreting background signal data, and that future analyses take this into account to avoid overinterpreting the data. With upcoming gravitational wave detectors capable of finding background signals more easily, it is essential to factor in the possible existence of heavy particles to avoid misleading conclusions about the universe's early stages.

Our research investigates the interaction of helical swimmers with multiple particles near a wall in a two-dimensional environment. We find that their unique swimming pattern creates a snowman-like effect, where their motion is impeded by adjacent particles due to an unexpected alignment. Furthermore, we discover that this snowman-like effect has a significant impact on the helical swimmers' ability to move forward, causing them to become stuck in compact clusters. Additionally, we examine how the helical swimmers' motion is affected by their chirality and the presence of an adjacent particle with the opposite handedness. We also analyze how the swimmers' speed and direction are influenced by the snowman-like effect in different scenarios.

This study explores the hamming distance dynamics in co-evolutionary genetic algorithms, focusing on Nash Equilibrium learning strategies both with individual and social learning. Our findings show that the hamming distance in the social learning case remains relatively stable, unlike the individual learning case which exhibits greater instability. This difference in dynamics is attributed to reduced exploration in the social learning scheme. Our analysis also reveals an interesting duality between social learning's hamming distance and individual learning's fitness values. In addition, our results highlight the significant impact of the learning parameter on hamming distance and fitness distance. Further, our study demonstrates that the hamming distance distribution under social learning can be approximated using a normal distribution, while the fitness values under individual learning follow a distribution that can be approximated by the Weibull distribution. Our research identifies potential areas for future study, including potential relationships between the learning parameter, hamming distance, and fitness values, and the potential application of our findings to other evolutionary computation methods.

The rapid evolution of external knowledge among adversaries poses a challenge for national security, complicating the ability to track the development of malicious ideas throughout texts. To tackle this issue, we develop an innovative technique called Security Concept Graph (SecConGraph), which uses Bidirectional LSTMs to accurately identify and organize security concepts within texts by modeling the relationships between ideas. We demonstrate the effectiveness of SecConGraph by successfully deploying it on two diverse datasets, the one derived from the Adversarial Knowledge Dynamics dataset and another from a publicly accessible dataset of terrorist plots. In both instances, SecConGraph exhibits a notable advantage over existing methods in both task and metric assessments. Furthermore, we uncover valuable insights about SecConGraph's performance by conducting comprehensive analyses of evaluation metrics and saliency maps. Ultimately, SecConGraph showcases the potential for dynamic knowledge tracking and provides a foundation for exploring solutions to this complex problem.

We introduce a new mixed opinion formation model that combines elements from the Schelling and Ising models. This hybrid model is particularly interesting because it allows us to extract the average magnetization from any initial condition, a feature that is generally challenging to achieve in dynamic systems. Notably, we have found that the average magnetization in this mixed model is closely linked to that of a pure Ising model, which is a significant observation given the Schelling model's segregation tendencies. As a result, the average magnetization may provide valuable insights into the dynamics of this hybrid system. To facilitate these findings, we have developed an alternative representation of the average magnetization that is more easily analyzable and can be applied even in large-scale systems. Additionally, our work is accompanied by an analytical study, which includes an in-depth examination of this new perspective and an exploration of the system's behavior at both small and infinite temperatures.

We've developed an original model to investigate the spread of COVID-19 infections through respiratory droplets, combining factors like weather conditions and air pollution. Our approach incorporates a multi-layer transport equation that divides the atmosphere into distinct layers based on droplet sizes, with discrete boundaries. We've tailored the model to fit specific environmental conditions and geographic locations, using historical temperature and humidity data to inform its parameters. We've also adapted the model to account for various transport methods, including gravity-driven flow, turbulent diffusion, and wind-carried movement, and have conducted a stability analysis to assess its effectiveness. To overcome computational challenges in solving the multi-layer system, we've developed a method to approximate the solution as a coupled system of ordinary and partial differential equations. We've tested the model in various environmental scenarios and demonstrated its ability to predict similar trends in droplet dispersion as observed in scientific research, and have applied it to analyze the spread of COVID-19 infections in different cities. The model has been implemented on high-performance computing clusters and is available online as an interactive tool enabling users to configure and run simulations for their own use cases.

The convergence of deep learning methods with rigorous mathematical foundations is a topic of current research interest. This work demonstrates the ability of a specific neural network to accurately solve notoriously difficult inverse and ill-posed problems, such as reconstructing images from raw sensor data and estimating parameters in complex dynamical systems from noisy and incomplete observations. By leveraging its ability to optimize a probabilistic model, the network addresses these challenges with relative ease, outperforming traditional methods despite their specific problem focus. The framework's ability to tackle a variety of tasks is also showcased through an experiment involving multiple image reconstruction applications. The associated code can be found at https://github.com/bkongsbak/NNforIP.

This study examines the equalities and inequalities between regular and symbolic powers of oriented edge ideals in weighted oriented graphs, building on existing research that established the equality between regular and symbolic powers of edge ideals in specific graph types, such as unweighted directed graphs and weighted undirected graphs. Our findings specifically address the challenges posed by graph structures with isolated vertices and parallel edges.

Using the holographic duality, we calculate the partition functions for SU(N) and U(N) in a variety of geometries, confirming existing formulas and yielding novel results. Our analysis particularly explores the subtle difference between the SU(N) and U(N) partition functions as N approaches infinity, revealing an intriguing disparity that stems from distinct boundary conditions affecting the bulk admissible states.

Deep neural networks widely apply quantization techniques, a form of silent data corruption, to speed up computations and reduce memory requirements. Our research reveals a critical flaw in uniform and non-uniform representation methods: they systematically discard data information. We argue that explicit mitigation strategies are necessary to address the silent data corruption issue. Focusing on energy-efficient designs utilizing finned hardware, we propose unconventional usage patterns where finite word lengths are optimized to minimize data losses. Finned hardware's variability is both input and weight-dependent, requiring distinct representation methods. We evaluated two different methods: one based on hardware values and the other on data entropy. Both approaches reduced data losses, resulting in a significant decrease in silent data corruption. The results showed both techniques effectively minimized data losses, with the entropy-based approach yielding improved accuracy in challenging finned hardware scenarios.

We've developed original graph-based algorithms to resolve two complex problems encountered in economic systems: finding optimal netting configurations and determining fair prices for settling debts. Our approaches leverage weighted graph theory to represent financial transactions and debts between economic entities. For the former challenge, we've created two strategies: one for calculating the Maximum Weighted Independent Set (MWIS) and another for the Maximum Weighted Degree Subgraph (MWDG). Our MWIS algorithm offers a suboptimal but easier-to-compute solution, while the MWDG approach can handle larger scales. For the latter challenge, we've investigated two methods to fairly settle debts: one based on Maximum Weighted Subgraph (MWS) and another focused on Maximum Weighted Degree Subgraph (MWDG). Our research demonstrated the degree of debt settlement, represented by the maximum weighted degree subgraph, can ensure the stability and fairness of economic equilibrium.

We explore the properties of a generalized Jordanian twist that arises from a specific deformation of the Yang-Baxter equation, known as the quantum Yang-Baxter equation. Our study reveals that this generalized twist can be expressed as a product of the simple Jordanian twist and another element that is ad-invariant. Consequently, both the generalized and simple Jordanian twists share the ability to generalize $R$-matrix and $F$-matrix properties. Ultimately, our research demonstrates the equivalence between these two twists, thereby indicating that the simple Jordanian twist is essentially the most fundamental form of a Jordanian twist.

This study introduces an innovative technique for identifying names in low-resource languages, significantly enhancing the performance in such conditions and offering a fully automatic and rule-free method for naming entity recognition. By leveraging the structural characteristics of names within sentences and incorporating a score-based loss function to handle label imbalance, our proposed model achieves notable success. Our evaluation utilizes the MultiWorld Names Corpus, a diverse and limited dataset, and our results demonstrate substantial improvements over both baseline models and current state-of-the-art NER techniques, with our model's scores surpassing them by 11.4% and 14.4% in F1-score respectively, while also exhibiting robustness to external influence through data augmentation.

Our research offers initial observations concerning particle ratios obtained in experiments conducted by ALICE, ATLAS, CMS, and CMS at the CERN, specifically for collisions involving lead ions at 5 TeV and corresponding collisions involving smaller scales of 5.02 TeV, 5.16 TeV, 5.44 TeV, 5.02 TeV, 5.44 TeV, 8.16 TeV, 8.16 TeV, 8.16 TeV, 8.16 TeV, 8.16 TeV, and 8.16 TeV. These findings relate to measurements of particle production, specifically for charged particles, pions, protons, and kappa mesons, and focus on discoveries made at the LHC's energy levels and its initial and intermediate stages. Compared to previous research conducted at lower energy levels, our study reveals an enhanced sensitivity to variations in particle ratios as collisions scale up from smaller to larger systems. Furthermore, our study reveals an intriguing variation in particle ratios at larger system scales, specifically for variations observed at the LHC's energy levels.

The success of dialogue state tracking (DST) models heavily relies on labeled data, but real-world datasets often contain mislabeled data that can harm performance. We investigate the impact of noisy data on DST models and develop a strong baseline for the DST task from data with accurate labels. Our research focuses on the GLUE dataset, which contains poorly labeled data and is unsuitable for DST. We created two clean datasets, one with 1990 labeled data and the other with 5900 labeled data, by carefully selecting reliable labels from a pool of 50000 annotated data. Our findings reveal that popular DST models are highly influenced by noisy data and can be improved through the use of data augmentation and robust training. Notably, our work highlights significant label noise in the Dialog-State Tracking Challenge dataset.

The intricate interconnectivity of a city's infrastructure and its inhabitants' social connections can have a notable impact on the spread of phenomena such as riots and the resulting influence on local government policy. To effectively model this process, we need to incorporate multiple factors including the structural features of the network, its dynamics during periods of unrest, and its effect on decision-making. In this paper, we introduce a new approach that rapidly evaluates different network configurations, observes alternative dynamics during periods of unrest, and, in an innovative move, includes an adaptive decision-making component responsive to changing network conditions. This novel methodology, based on multi-agent systems and adaptive control theory, allows us to generate precise guidelines for optimizing network structure to minimize conflict and promote civic peace in the presence of unrest. Additionally, this model can provide valuable insights into the optimal distribution of resources, such as law enforcement, in responding to unrest in a timely and effective manner.

Our investigation aims to evaluate the precision of star formation rate estimates produced by the Prospector's Bayesian inference framework, specifically exploring its sensitivity to assumptions about galaxy formation and how it relates to observables. To accomplish this, we create a dataset of 220 galaxies with various spectroscopic measurements that have a high level of consistency and use the Prospector to determine their star formation histories and mass-to-light ratios. A key aspect of our analysis involves assessing the precision of derived quantities, including the star formation rates, which is influenced by parameters such as line strength and spectral energy distribution details. We find that the Precise Measurements of Absolute Luminosities of Bethe (Betra) are a strong indicator of precision for star formation rates and a weak indicator for mass-to-light ratios. Furthermore, we find that the line strength and Betra are key factors that influence the precision of star formation rates and that the line strength has the most significant impact. Additionally, we find that the line strength and Betra are more effective in assessing the precision of star formation rates than other factors such as scatter in the relation between line strength and star formation rate or galaxy type. We find that the line strength and Betra are correlated with the scatter in the relation between line strength and star formation rate or galaxy type. We find that the line strength and Betra are correlated with the scatter in the relation between line strength and star formation rate or galaxy type. We provide an inequality for the maximum number of polynomials in a sum of squares decomposition, which corresponds to the rank of matrices within the Gram spectrahedron for polynomial rings over the complex numbers or the real numbers. This inequality leads to a computable certificate for the non-negative definiteness of a matrix in the Gram spectrahedron when the underlying variable space is bounded. Additionally, we offer a bounded version of the Lasserre relaxation that is equivalent to the original optimization problem when the variable space is unbounded.

The FASERν experiment, situated near the end of the AXIONLENS-50 km straight section at the HL-LHC, will investigate neutrino interactions by observing secondary ν μ and ν τ neutrino populations generated from μ ± and τ ± decay. When operating during the ATLAS HL-LHC run, FASERν has the capability of providing significant constraints on leptonic unitarity violation, complementing existing CKM unitarity violation limits. With an expected annual luminosity of 3 AB-1 at 13 TeV, FASERν is anticipated to place stringent constraints on both real and virtual scalar fields discarding parts of the parameter space not covered by existing theoretical bounds, with real scalar fields constrained to a mass range of over 10 GeV and virtual scalar fields constrained to above 4 GeV.

Brzozowski's operator for regular expressions was initially introduced as an inverse counterpart to the Kleene star, and it has been shown to form a group with star that constitutes a complete and consistent set of algebraic manipulations for regular expressions. Despite its utility in modifying regular expressions, the fair derivative of a regular expression, obtained via Brzozowski's operator, has been found to be an important component in designing a symbolic decision procedure for regular expression containment. The procedure involves checking whether one regular expression is contained within another and can be accomplished through the computation of the fair derivative. The purpose of this research is to enhance the computational efficiency of the fair derivative of a regular expression by providing an optimized algorithm that, under specific conditions, can bypass the need for the complete derivation. The proposed algorithm can be viewed as a partial derivative solver that gives preferred elements as input and produces preferred derivatives as output. The algorithm represents a significant improvement as it results in considerable computational time reductions, as demonstrated by the regular expression containment instances it has been tested with. The algorithm is also universally applicable and does not depend on a specific regular expression pattern.

Deep learning-based Visual-Inertial Odometry (VIO) models have successfully achieved high accuracy in real-time pose estimation by leveraging the power of deep neural networks to combine and process visual and inertial data. Unlike traditional VIO algorithms, which utilize optimization-based methods to estimate the pose and camera motion, deep learning-based VIO models use implicit representations of the system's state and motion. Despite the implicit state representation, research has shown that deep learning-based VIO models can accurately estimate the absolute orientation, a challenging task for traditional VIO algorithms. This paper provides a comprehensive survey of deep learning-based VIO models, including a systematic characterization of their architecture, state representation, motion representation, training, optimization, and implementation techniques. Furthermore, we delve into the advantages and limitations of these models and explore their performance in various scenarios.

Building upon the lower-dimensional theory, we label higher-order Weyl semimetals as "square-root topological insulators" and describe their fundamental characteristics in 3D systems. A specific formula links the interlayer coupling to the Weyl point's location, temperature, and Fermi level in the quadratic expansion of the free energy. Additionally, we explore two examples - transition metal trihalides and carbon monoboron - and employ both experimental and calculated methods to determine their square-root topological invariants. Verification of these theories is advocated through precise measurements of thermal conductivity, anomalous Hall conductivity, and interlayer coupling in transition metal trihalides.

This study examines the effectiveness of edge finite elements in solving a data recovery problem, specifically a continuous Galerkin discrete identifiability problem. We investigate the impact of various edge elements on the numerical solution, comparing conforming and nonconforming elements with increasing degree up to two. Our analysis employs a specific example and a specialized identifiability tool to assess the convergence of solutions. Our results demonstrate that the choice of edge elements can significantly influence the numerical solution, with some elements failing to yield convergent solutions even with higher-order precision. However, our findings also indicate that certain nonconforming edge elements can provide stable solutions comparable to their conforming counterparts. Ultimately, our research emphasizes the crucial role that edge elements play in data recovery problems and highlights the need for further studies on the properties of nonconforming elements in this context.

This paper delves into the properties of the parafermion vertex operator algebra for the affine Lie superalgebra $osp(1|2n)$, specifically identifying its associated generators and determining the irreducible highest weight modules within the category $\mathcal{O}$. Additionally, the paper establishes an equivalence between this category and a category of integrable highest weight modules for the simple affine Lie algebra $A_{2n}^{(1)}$, facilitated by the use of vertex operator algebra automorphisms.

We introduce a novel approach that simplifies the student model training process, reducing the need for explicit rejection sampling. Our saliency-based approach identifies and isolates key aspects of the teacher model's knowledge, making it more efficient to train a student model. In essence, we're proposing a method to bypass the inherent noise in the teacher models' outputs, thereby bypassing the rejection sampling process. By doing so, we can directly train the student model to match the identified key aspects of the teacher models' knowledge, resulting in a more streamlined training process. In experiments, we demonstrate that our approach achieves comparable performance to the original method using augmented data, with a significant reduction in training time.

Previous research suggested that grid cells contribute to the brain's internal compass system by providing location information that resists external influence. However, our findings reveal that entorhinal cortex grid cells adapt their angular periodicity based on visual cues and movement directions learned through associative learning. This suggests that grid cells' inherent stability is tempered by their connection to wider sensory-motor integration networks. Additionally, our results indicate that hippocampal place cells' response to learning and memory are facilitated by the interplay between multiple sensory inputs and the movement-related influences on grid cells, the latter being an unexpected factor.

The development of a star's magnetic cycle is significantly influenced by the kinematic dynamo sector, particularly in low-rotation rate stars. The Wulfman mechanism, which drives the dynamo, is the subject of this study. We examine how the kinematic dynamo's cycle generation capability is affected by angular momentum transportation across interface regions in solar-like stars. This research expands upon previous models by incorporating the Umov-Poynting vector and energy transport equations to predict heat transport patterns. It also introduces an empirical boundary regime model to account for strong interactions at interface regions. The results show that cycle generation in these stars is highly sensitive to heat transport and interface interactions, and that turbulent heat transport can significantly impact dynamo cycle lengths. However, even in this case, the kinematic sector's cycle length is still primarily determined by interface transport and rotation rate.

We start by identifying all quartic extensions in the S4 group, with discriminant $\Delta \leq -200$, up to a certain field size. Then, we analyze how these extensions interact with a specific family of elliptic curves, gaining rank when combined. We impose additional constraints on this family, relating their ranks to the ideals within the quartic extensions. Ultimately, we find that either there are infinitely many cases where the ranks of the elliptic curves are zero, or there are finite alternatives. If the latter, we determine the specific cases. If the former, we conjecture that the infinite cases result from anti-symmetric rational points on the elliptic curves.

We examine the time-dependent density-density correlation function and entropy production after a system undergoes a quantum quench from an equilibrium state described by the Gaudin-Huberman theorem. In particular, we investigate the relationship between the change in entropy, temperature, and the heat production during this process. We demonstrate that the irreversibility of this process is reflected in the initial increase in entropy and temperature, which ultimately decreases over time as the system settles into its new equilibrium state. We establish a precise connection between these quantities, citing the role of the total entropy and temperature in determining the steady-state configuration. We establish an explicit relationship between the change in entropy, temperature, and heat production, which is derived from the first law of thermodynamics and the definition of entropy. This relationship takes the form of an equality involving the initial and final thermodynamic state parameters, the heat production, and the work done during the quench. This equality can be represented as an entropy diagram, offering an intuitive visual understanding of the entropy production, heat production, work done, and related quantities during a quantum quench. We introduce an explicit example based on the XXZ spin chain to provide concrete numerical data for these relationships.

We investigate the time it takes for a combined system and environment to lose distinguishability from a given reference state, examining both unitary and non-unitary dynamics using the time-twirling approach. For unitary evolution, we show that this time indeed increases with the system's interaction time, as predicted by the Haghi-Huelga-Vidal proposal, and that it serves as an upper bound for the geometric mean of the system's entanglement time and the environment's entanglement time. For non-unitary processes, we find that the time-twirling approach still provides a valid upper bound for the geometric mean of the system's decay time and the environment's decay time. Furthermore, we find that this time-twelling approach can be bounded from below by the longest decay time among the system and environment, leading to it being indeterminate in unitary dynamics.

We investigate the existence of a nondegenerate regular simplex within the unit cube $Q_n$ with side length $s$ that contains $n$ interpolation nodes associated with functions in the $l_1^d$ space. For the case where $d \geq 2$, we demonstrate that such a simplex exists provided that $s \geq \sqrt{d(n-1)}$; conversely, we prove that for any $d \geq 1$ and $n \geq 3$, there is no such simplex when $s < \sqrt{d(n-1)}$. Additionally, we derive an upper bound on the smallest eigenvalue of the Gramian matrix built from the nodes within the simplest case ($d=1$).

We examined the surface conduction of two types of silicon surfaces that have been etched with hydrogen peroxide: silicon etched from a carrier concentration and silicon etched from an oxide concentration.  Our research showed that etched silicon surfaces conduct electricity quickly, but also noted a significant decrease in their conductivity when compared to oxide etched silicon surfaces.  Additionally, our findings indicated that the high conductivity of etched silicon can be both a benefit and a drawback, depending on how it is applied.  We derived mathematical equations to describe the distribution of charge on etched silicon surfaces and verified these with our experimental results.  Our model also showed that the thickness of the depletion region on etched silicon surfaces is directly proportional to the square root of the reverse bias applied.  We believe that our research will be useful in further exploring the properties and enhancing the performance of etched silicon surfaces.

This paper contributes to the long-term goal of establishing connections between twisted topological K-theory and motivic cohomology. We demonstrate the implications of cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted homotopy K-theory, confirming these formulations for projective schemes in dimensions $\le 2$. To this end, we establish cdh descent and Milnor excision for twisted homotopy K-theory by building on the framework of Kahn-Kassabian-Kapronov. Additionally, we demonstrate the isomorphism $\tilde{K}^i(X,j)_j \cong H^{i+1}(X)_j$ for open subsets $X$ within $\mathbb{A}^n_{\text{et}}$, assuming $X$ is nonempty, for $n\le 2$ or for any $n$ with $X$ connected.

The evolution of a planet's atmosphere, whether it's a terrestrial or gaseous planet, is greatly impacted by its interior and exterior components working in a cyclical manner. This planetary system process, which involves the recycling of materials between the core, mantle, and atmosphere, drives forward the evolution of the planet's internal and external features. It influences how elements are distributed and rearranged within the planet, shaping the atmosphere's composition and the interior's structure. This paper delves into the computational tools being used to model atmospheric evolution, discussing the methods for calculating material cycling rates and retaining times. It also explores how these processes work in conjunction with internal processes to dictate the composition of planets. Furthermore, the article examines the various factors that affect atmospheric evolution, including processes that renew the atmosphere, influence gas grip releases, and affect heat flux and mantle convection. Ultimately, this model is applied to study the evolution of hydrogen-dominated atmospheres on gas giants.

Our experiments using the CIDS method on 1,2-propanediol (1,2-PDO) and 1,3-propanediol (1,3-PDO) reveal distinct outcomes for these diols, which differ significantly in their chemical properties. Although both molecules can produce methyl cations, our findings show that 1,2-PDO is more efficient in this process. Our data indicate that the 1,2-PDO dissociation dynamic involves a initial one-electron transfer followed by a proton transfer, resulting in the formation of a methyl cation and a hydroxyl anion. In contrast, 1,3-PDO primarily undergoes proton transfer, producing water as a product. Our results also highlight the importance of considering inner-shell electrons when analyzing CIDS spectra, as an initial one-electron transfer is a crucial step in the 1,2-PDO dissociation dynamic.

Quantum circuit simulations offer a promising route to exploring tensor networks through the application of quantum algorithms, with the potential to exploit classical compression techniques. We present a general approach to translating common tensor networks - specifically matrix product states and valence bond solid states - into quantum circuits, demonstrating that this conversion yields circuits whose depth is significantly lower than randomly generated equivalents. Using this circuit representation, we successfully solve the tensor network time-evolution problem using the quantum circuit algorithm QAOA, with impressive results showing that deep time-evolution problems can be solved with relatively shallow circuits. Notably, our strategy offers a precise means of controlling the complexity of tensor networks during time-evolution, an important feature that has yet to be achieved with stochastic algorithms.

The classification of tumor morphology holds significant potential for cancer diagnosis and treatment planning. Conventionally, this classification is achieved through the analysis of histopathological images with traditional machine learning methods. Recently, graph neural networks have demonstrated exceptional performance in this task by capturing complex tumor morphologies. However, these models are often hindered by over-reliance on domain expertise due to the need for manually extracted node and graph features. To overcome this limitation, we propose an end-to-end framework called DeepTissueType, which utilizes a graph neural network called Variational Graph Neural Network (VGNN) to classify tissue samples by learning the features of the tumor and surrounding tissue from raw image data. Additionally, we demonstrate the advantages of our method over traditional approaches using the FigCap dataset and show that DeepTissueType achieves a classification accuracy of 73.11%, outperforming existing methods on the dataset.

This research extends the linear Hawkes process to a nonlinear form that can effectively model interactions in complex systems, such as networks of events with varied influences, by proposing the Ricker Hawkes process. The nonlinear Hawkes process can be categorized as an exponential Hawkes process, and we explore its fundamental properties, including the stability of a general exponential process, the specific parameters of the Ricker process, and its detailed analysis. Furthermore, we examine the accuracy of our nonlinear model in predicting future events and assess its performance using simulated data. The results demonstrate that the Ricker process outperforms the linear Hawkes model in a significant number of cases.

We've introduced an open-source, adaptive, N-body simulation tool called Enzo-DarkGravity to enhance the computational speed of massive astrophysical simulations involving gravity. This framework, based on the Fast Multipole Method (FMM), adapts the method's complexity to match the density distribution of the system, optimizing performance for a wide range of simulations. By efficiently calculating gravitational forces, even in dense, self-gravitating systems, Enzo-DarkGravity can significantly reduce computation time compared to traditional direct force calculations. This advancement enables more adaptive simulations with better resolution across multiple scales, making it particularly beneficial for modeling galaxy evolution and correcting the stellar energy spectrum in massive, dense cores.

Cross-domain adaptation is a crucial issue in medical image segmentation due to varying image qualities, patient populations, and imaging modalities. We propose a contrastive semi-supervised learning method for cross-anatomy domain adaptation, namely C.S.-C.A.D.A., which employs a contrastive loss function and two adaptation networks to leverage unlabeled samples from both source and target domains. Our method integrates two main components: a contrastive loss function that enhances the robustness of the model by training it to distinguish between sample pairs from the same domain and those from different domains; and two adaptation networks that compress the domain difference by training them on the combined samples from both source and target domains, resulting in a more compact and domain-invariant representation. By converging the two networks through a contrastive learning approach, C.S.-C.A.D.A. can achieve a more precise representation of the common anatomy across domains. Ultimately, our model achieves superior performance in semi-supervised medical image segmentation tasks, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods by 5.03% in terms of Dice score on a real-world brain segmentation dataset.

We provide evidence that a comprehensive understanding of four-dimensional supersymmetric gravity can be achieved through a revised perspective on supergravity that incorporates the principles of BRS symmetry. We offer a revised perspective on supergravity that eliminates unnecessary components in the gravitational multiplet, while introducing additional components in the gravitino multiplet. We demonstrate that the revised structure results in a consistent and renormalizable theory, fulfilling the criteria of BRS invariance, and that the modified superhelicity formula for the gravitino now accurately reflects the proper helicity degree for a massless gravitino. Furthermore, we establish that the BRS invariance of the full supergravity theory enables the creation of a massive gravitino, thereby challenging the conventional view that a massless gravitino is required to maintain the consistency of the theory.

To overcome limitations in plasma devices, such as plasma cut-offs in lasers for inertial confinement or the restriction on magnetic field strength, researchers have proposed using plasma waveplates. These waveplates can modify the polarization of waves while maintaining their intensity, although their effectiveness relies on precise control of plasma conditions. A specific type of plasma waveplate has been shown to change the polarization of microwave or laser waves by rotating them up to $\pi/2$ when subjected to a transverse magnetic field. However, this function is only achieved when the plasma layer has a thickness greater than or equal to one centimeter, which is influenced by both the electron density in the plasma and the magnetic field's strength. A theoretical analysis and experimental evidence demonstrate that this type of plasma waveplate can also shift the position of circularly polarized waves, rotating them by $\pi/2$ and changing their left-right handedness. Consequently, this suggests that plasma waveplates could be used to study circularly polarized photons and enable control over the polarization and position of waves.

We examine the electric dipole moment of the tau lepton within the type-II two-Higgs doublet model, focusing on its sensitivity to the CP-violating phases within the framework of general relativity. Our analysis considers the constraints imposed by experimental limits on the Higgs boson mass, the tau electric dipole moment, and the muon anomalous magnetic moment, as well as constraints derived from the stability of the vacuum and the avoidance of too rapid proton decay. Our findings reveal that the type-II two-Higgs doublet model exhibits sensitivity to the tau electric dipole moment, with values potentially reaching $10^{-18}$ ecm, although this depends on the mass of the lighter Higgs boson and the phase of the type-II parameter $\tan\beta$.

This paper delves into the error correction capabilities of rank metric codes, specifically codes defined by two metrics: the rank metric and the Hamming metric. We examine decoding strategies that minimize the Hamming weight of erroneous messages following a rank metric error, considering constraints on code parameters, particularly the dimension of the ambient space. Notably, we establish that for low-to-medium error rates, sparse codes can be almost surely correctly identified by minimal Hamming weight, while for higher error rates or larger code densities, the same level of performance is achieved only on average. This distinction highlights the limitations of rank metric codes for rates below and above 1/2. We further prove that there are sequences of good rank metric codes with optimal gap rates, both for large-rate codes with minimal Hamming weight errors and low-to-medium-rate codes with minimal Hamming weight errors, for specific dimensions of the ambient space that approach the capacity of the binary erasure channel. This finding demonstrates the effectiveness of rank metric codes for achieving high data compression factors near the BEC capacity.

The structure of conserved current block expansions in two-dimensional conformal field theory is re-examined through the lens of AdS$_2$ geodesic operators, leading to an intriguing paradox that suggests a deeper connection with the Higgs mechanism. To resolve this paradox, the perspective is shifted towards the conserved current block itself, with the aim of describing it in a way that is independent of the geometric framework. By doing so, the apparent duality between AdS$_2$ geodesic operators and their counterparts in three dimensions can be understood, revealing that the representation of conserved current block expansions in CFT$_2$ differs when expressed with AdS$_3$ geodesic operators as it does with AdS$_2$ when considering massless fields in CFT$_2$. The resolution of this paradox has significant implications for our comprehension of the holographic principle and AdS/CFT correspondence, while the direct relationship between geodesic operators in AdS$_2$ and AdS$_3$ provides new insight into the nature of conserved currents within the context of AdS$_3$ CFT$_2$, notably for the AdS$_3$ boundary value problem recently addressed by Castello, Grallert, and Jevickova.

Using the Halofit model, we predict the distribution of galaxy shear in the Hubble Space Telescope's COSMOS field. Our analysis evaluates the performance of neural network and traditional estimators on near-future galaxy surveys. Specifically, we assess the crushers' ability to reconstruct lensing maps and estimate the mass-over-radius of dark matter as a function of halo mass. Our key findings indicate that neural networks can potentially achieve similar results to traditional methods with much fewer galaxies. Furthermore, we predict a slight improvement in the estimation of mass-over-radius when employing neural networks.

In 2000, David Eisenbud introduced the concept of combinatorial differential manifolds within the context of his research on differential operators. Over a decade later, Eisenbud and his colleagues further developed this research, addressing associated properties and abstract differential operators in 2013. This paper builds upon their findings, exploring the relationship between combinatorial differential manifolds and monoidal category structures. Additionally, the paper presents a demonstration of the applicability of this theory to fields of mathematics, including algebraic geometry and differential geometry.

The Type II supernova SN~2020jfo had an exceptionally long and stable [Ni~II] line peak around 140~days post-explosion. To understand the nickel and iron ejection patterns, we obtained medium-resolution spectroscopy with the VLT/XSHUT at 246~days. The new data showed a 3000~km/s iron absorption line in the pre-heated, high-density gas surrounding the nickel core. Compared to other Type II supernovae, SN~2020jfo has a notably higher nickel-to-iron mass ratio, about five times larger than the solar value. This ratio is consistent with the predictions of one-dimensional stellar explosion models. The iron in SN~2020jfo's spectrum is about ten times more abundant than nickel in mass, but their energy contributions under specific wavelength ranges differ substantially. As a result, both optical and near-infrared light curves were significantly influenced, with SN~2020jfo exhibiting a delayed peak and extended tail due to its distinct nickel and iron distributions.

A cross-like image is produced when using a point source with an off-axis lobster-eye optics configuration. Researchers demonstrated mathematically and experimentally that this cross-like image has specific properties. By analyzing the rotation angle of the cross, they were able to determine which part of the optics system the image corresponded to. As a result, this rotation angle can be used to identify specific components of the optics system, such as the entrance and exit pupils, and the point of focus. Additionally, this rotation angle can indicate system malfunctions, such as asymmetry. Consequently, this research provides a way to assess the balance and proper functioning of lobster-eye optics systems.

We employ level set methods in conjunction with technique switches to develop an efficient algorithm for solving second-order fully nonlinear partial differential equations, notably the equation $u_t + F(t,x,u,Nu) + \lambda = 0$ that is given in implicit form. The algorithm leverages an operator splitting approach and the Lagrange multiplier method to overcome challenges posed by singular coefficients and fully nonlinear terms. A flexible scheme design allows for multiple technique switches within a single time step, enabling both monotone and consistency properties. Although the algorithm may generate intermediate solutions outside its desired domain, it maintains the ability to precisely track the level set function, utilizing which we derive an efficient and straightforward approach to regain domain consistency. Consequently, the algorithm yields solutions for the implicit equation, addressing a notable shortfall in prior research. We validate the algorithm's effectiveness through numerical experiments and ease of implementation on both single-core and multi-core processors.

Using the COCO suite of simulations with varying parameters including the amplitude of initial scalar perturbations $\sigma_8$, we examine how accurately a deep learning model derived from density data alone can predict the mass of halos within a specific redshift and mass range. The simulations indicate that even when density fluctuations are held constant, the model erratically estimates halo masses due to an inability to account for variations in the power spectrum of matter fluctuations $\Delta^2_k$. Consequently, when increasing $\sigma_8$ by 0.4 in simulations with $\sigma_8=0.7$, the model inaccurately estimates a $34\%$ mean magnitude halo mass for $M \approx \10^11\,M_\odot$ at $z=0.5$, a value that is particularly susceptible to additional variations in $\Delta^2_k$.

Our research offers a semi-supervised version of the Convolutional Neural Matrix Factorization (CNMF) method, adapted for piano transcription. This adapted method competes favorably with high-performing low-rank factorization techniques and sophisticated deep learning methods, especially when paired with a suitable hyperparameter tuning method, as we've demonstrated in our CNMF-related experiments. Additionally, our approach achieves significant improvements in music transcription accuracy using only piano audio, a challenging task with a large gap in performance according to our assessment. We've obtained the code and data for our semi-supervised CNMF and hyperparameter tuning method at https://github.com/colson1993/piano-transcription-cnmf.

This research introduces a novel approach to assigning properties like mass, angular momentum, and entropy to individual fluid elements within stars that rotate. Unlike conventional methods, this new assignment standardizes these properties by averaging them on small, circular paths (isopersons) that align with the star's rotation cycle. Compared to traditional methods, isoperson-based properties reveal more distinct patterns and are less dispersed, especially in regions near the star's poles and equator.
