To better understand rotating stars composed of fluids with varying properties, this research provides an applicable framework that uses isoperson-based assignments. Finally, this research demonstrates the usefulness of isoperson-based properties by re-examining previous studies on rotating stars in various scenarios.

The cost of acquiring labeled data is significantly lowered through selective labeling, a proven technique for enhancing training models. Selective labeling achieves this cost reduction by only labeling specific, strategically chosen data points from a larger pool of unlabeled information. The key challenge in effectively utilizing selective labeling lies in identifying the most valuable data points that should be labeled to maximize the potential for model improvement. The problem of selective labeling is further complicated in deep learning systems by the presence of a feedback loop between the model and data, making it necessary to analyze the problem in an integrated manner. This paper examines the benefits of selective labeling in deep learning and reviews a variety of methods that aim to identify the most beneficial data points for labeling. It also highlights the advantages and limitations of each approach and explores potential areas for future improvement.

The merger of two neutron stars or a neutron star and a black hole's merger produces neutron stars that emit electromagnetic and gravitational waves in a process known as a neutron star coalescence. Observing these events through both electromagnetic and gravitational wave observations enriches our understanding of them. While gravitational wave observations provide information about the merger's shape, size, and orientation, electromagnetic observations offer insights into the proton-to-electron ratio in the post merger context. Researchers have analyzed data from neutron star coalescences, including GW190814, to determine the minimum detectable proton-to-electron ratio. They found that neutron star mergers produce substantial amounts of electron/proton plasma with relatively high thresholds of 10^-5 times the threshold of the standard electron/proton ratio. Additionally, restrictions on dark matter's influence through scalar dark matter were imposed, with results showing that dark matter doesn't significantly impact neutron star mergers unless it has a mass density five orders of magnitude lower than previously estimated limits. Researchers also set upper limits on dark matter's influence on gravitational wave amplitude, ending up with constraints on dark matter's influence on gravitational wave amplitude, ending up with constraints on dark matter's influence on gravitational wave amplitude at 0.25 times its previously estimated limits.

Effective public health policies necessitate a thorough comprehension of the social determinants of health, which are rooted in individual experiences and habits shaped by personal and environmental factors.  A vast amount of valuable, yet underutilized data resides within clinical notes in healthcare systems.  Utilizing natural language processing and machine learning, we developed a robust method for extracting from clinical notes details on patients' lifestyles, living conditions, and health status.  By implementing this on a substantial dataset of clinical notes from the MIMIC-III database, we successfully created a comprehensive patient profile that accurately reflected various social determinants of health and enabled noticeable advancements in predicting important healthcare outcomes like readmission and mortality.

We have examined the problem of minimizing the time it takes to move a variable-dimension swimmer, subject to oscillating position constraints, between two fixed locations. We demonstrated that this problem can be rewritten as a problem of optimizing a piecewise-linear cost function in two dimensions. We then established the existence and uniqueness of a minimum cost in this space. To further analyze this problem, we introduced a discrete model featuring the swimmer switching between different dimension modes at regular intervals. We proved that as the switching frequency increases, the optimal solution approaches the optimal solution of the continuous-time control problem. We also established that the optimal solution of the piecewise-linear cost function can be realized through a suitable choice of costs associated with switching between different dimension modes. This understanding enables us to characterize the structure of the optimal policy in the original problem, leading to an explicit formula for the optimal cost. Additionally, we explored applications of this problem to two specific problem settings.

Our research explores the impact of the COVID-19 pandemic on community connections in Berlin from 2019 to 2021, using recreational sports participation as a metric. By analyzing changes in the diversity of urban encounters among athletes, we found that the pandemic led to a sharp decline in community connections in its initial stage. This decline continued through 2020 with fewer, more isolated athletes taking part in sports until the tail end of the year when restrictions were eased. In 2021, we observed an increase in community connections as vaccination rates improved and loosened guidelines allowed more athletes to engage in sports, resulting in a rise in diverse urban encounters. Notably, some athletic groups that saw significant growth during the pandemic, such as wheelchair basketball players, required special courts that were initially scarce, forcing them to compete with other teams for access. As the pandemic subsided, these communities continued to demonstrate resilience, with some clubs adapting to offer alternative programs to attract a broader, more diverse participant base, ensuring their long-term sustainability.

The extreme energy released by the strongest X-ray flares from V883 Omega, a recently transformed young star, has implications for the surrounding disc. Despite the large distance between the star and the CO snow line, a potential gap in the disc caused by the movement of ice particles and its effects on migration patterns remain unknown. Using computer simulations of the disc around V883 Omega, we found that the inner disc, influenced by the star's intense radiation and massive convective storms, maintains stability through differential rotation. However, a local instability near the star is prevented from releasing energy in the form of X-rays by its own convective mixing, shifting it instead into more stable forms like heat and turbulence. This arrangement allows the star to sustain a significant differential rotation rate, necessary for migrating objects to maintain the disc's stability through collisional dissipation of angular momentum.

We create an abstract formulation of scattering theory that is compatible with the squashing procedure, mirroring the characteristics of scattering matrices and asymptotic symmetries encountered in the AdS$_2$ context. This formulation effectively captures the essence of scattering processes in a systematic manner, allowing for an intuitive understanding of asymptotic symmetries and their associated charges within the framework of AdS$_2$ physics.

As 5G cellular towers spring up, people are expressing concern about possible health effects from increased exposure to radiofrequency energy. To assess this issue, researchers reviewed previous studies on exposure levels from 5G and 4G cellular towers. They developed mathematical models to estimate exposure levels, one of which accounted for how energy builds up within structures. Unlike many studies, which assume that structures act as barriers blocking radiofrequency energy, this model showed that buildings can actually facilitate energy transmission, perhaps by 10 to 20 times. Consequently, the distances at which radiofrequency energy starts to drop off become much more minimal. As a result, the maximum safe exposure distance, according to international guidelines, shortens substantially. In fact, at a recent conference, another researcher used this very model to estimate that, according to certain guidelines, the maximum safe exposure distance could drop as low as 0.89 feet.

This study presents a novel approach to measuring water surface elevation based on a jet-diffusion model, which incorporates an inverse method, particularly useful for analyzing irregular waves. By transforming the water surface profile into a one-dimensional signal, we can determine the wave phase and envelope using the jet-diffusion model. To achieve this, we employ an iterative fourier transform technique and a least-squares method to solve the inverse problem. Our method bypasses the need for fourier transform, making it applicable to non-periodic waves. We validate our approach through numerical simulations and comparative analyses with established methods, revealing it yields results closely aligned with the exact solution for monochromatic and soliton waves, and significantly outperforms other methods in accuracy for more complex wave types, including combinations of monochromatic and soliton waves, as measured by the error of the envelope and phase.

The surface layer theorem originally applies to differential forms under constant rank conditions and specifies how forms within a defined distance can be matched to those on a surface layer. This concept has been expanded to differential operators in general and forms with variable rank in locally convex spaces. A new proof focuses on the underlying topology, identifying a fundamental parameter that determines the validity of the surface layer theorem and its generalizations. This parameter is shown to influence the topological properties of the hom complex of continuous differential forms.

This paper presents an innovative, multi-layered control system for mobile platforms that utilizes sonar sensors to navigate in a unknown environment. We demonstrate the system's effectiveness by applying its components to two distinct challenges: avoiding obstacles in an open space and locating and escaping from a confined area. Our method met the criteria for Layered Control Reconfigurability, and our experiments used a custom-built robot to test its capabilities. The system's performance improvements show a significant boost in navigation capabilities, and our approach offers an enhanced sensing framework that surpasses traditional range-based methods.

The impact of contextual information on the effectiveness of deep learning models in identifying fake news has been a subject of research and debate. To address this issue, we present a comprehensive analysis involving six top-ranked models and a variety of contextual information levels in the Contextual Information Analysis for Fake News Detection (CIAFND) dataset. Our results from both single-task and multi-task learning experiments reveal that four models benefit from contextual information and that the best overall performance is achieved with contextual information at the medium level. Our findings also demonstrate that models with a tendency to overfit (high variance) perform better with less contextual information, whereas models with a tendency to underfit (low variance) perform better with more contextual information. Additionally, our analysis confirms the influence of model architecture on contextual information utilization but finds no correlation with model capacity. Ultimately, our study advocates for customized evaluation of deep learning models in the context of information diffusion tasks to account for contextual information.

A theoretical framework for understanding the hysteresis exhibited by systems in the presence of nonuniform entropy distribution has been developed, drawing inspiration from the Curie-Weiss model. This framework demonstrates that hysteresis arises when the system's connectivity exhibits a specific type of nonuniformity that we term "curvature effect," which arises even in the absence of external fields. Furthermore, our analysis reveals that the curvature effect has a profound impact on the system's behavior, influencing both its entropy and how it changes with temperature. In certain cases, the system's hysteresis pattern can be explained solely by its entropy distribution. Our research also identifies the conditions under which the system's connectivity gives rise to bistability and the corresponding values of the mean and half-width of the hysteresis loop. In addition, we find that the system's connectivity can be controlled through the exchange of heat with its surroundings, allowing the system's hysteresis to be fine-tuned. This is demonstrated through both analytical calculations and numerical simulations of the system's time-dependent response to changing temperature. Our results imply that the system's connectivity can store energy, which is a crucial aspect of magnetic hysteresis.

Our research offers an efficient suboptimal policy for selecting the decoding order that achieves nearly optimal performance while significantly reducing the complexity from O(n^2) to O(n log n) in comparison to the optimal brute force method. We introduce an innovative harmonic mean (HM) metric that effectively captures the joint error probability of dual BPSK modulations and utilizes this metric in our proposed algorithm. In line with information-theoretic optimality criteria, our method is also applicable to other modulation types such as QPSK and MPSK. In terms of performance, our results show a less than 0.1 dB penalty at a 10^-4 BER for dual BPSK and a less than 1 dB penalty for dual QPSK. We demonstrate the practicality of our approach through a simulation of dual BPSK and dual QPSK systems experiencing both fast and slow fading.

We introduce an innovative method for solving a complex optimization problem derived from L1-PCA, which generalizes the Classic PCA issue. The new challenge involves minimizing a data loss function, defined as the sum of the absolute deviations of squared differences between data points and their reconstructions, with additional rotational symmetry constraints placed on the reconstruction. The optimization process for this problem is made more manageable by transforming it into a two-block reformulated form, which can be solved using an alternating algorithm that first fixes one variable and solves a linear least squares problem for the other variable, and then applies a nonconvesive tangent skew-symmetric operator splitting preconditioned Newton method to solve the remaining smooth block. We demonstrate the effectiveness of our method through numerical experiments in clustering and angular subspace estimation scenarios.

We suggest a technique to validate annotated data consistency, which can be
efficiently integrated into any paraphrasing system. Our approach involves
measuring the degree of agreement between original and paraphrased annotations.
We demonstrate the practical applications of this method to paraphasing tasks
related to semantic labeling, which can be any task represented by a knowledge
graph, such as named entity recognition, part-of-speech tagging, and sentence
classification. Additionally, we present a technique to enhance annotation
consistency by incorporating both original and paraphrased annotations into
the training data. Our method is evaluated through the annotation of a dataset
called CLS-DT, which consists of Chinese text. Our results show that our method
can increase the annotation agreement among human annotators and also boost the
performance of a model when used to combine original and paraphrased annotations
for model training.

We demonstrate that the combination of prefix-independent half-positional objectives,
encompassing all parity and co-Büchi objectives, yields a positional winning condition.
This contrasts with a non-prefix-independent combination (specifically, the union of all
parity objectives) that cannot yield a half-positional condition greater than a reachability
objective. Furthermore, we show that fair-but-finite (FBF) automata can determine whether
a given game posits a half-positional winning condition, solving the half-positional query
problem for games. This solution exploits the union of all parity objectives inherent in
half-positional conditions and employs a novel, scalable intersection algorithm for Büchi
automata, applicable to FBF automata when the intersection result is finite.

X-ray spectra from the High Energy Spectroscopic System on the Chandra and the X-ray Multi-Mirror Mission-Newton have allowed for the examination of X-ray spectra in asynchronous polars, comprising the objects HH 332-1 (V454 Cas), HH 332-2 (V523 Cas), and the newly studied PX 1555-43.  Comparisons with standard polars reveal that asynchronous polars exhibit higher temperatures and greater mass accretion rates.  X-ray spectra of HH 332-1 and HH 332-2, which share similar temperatures and mass accretion rates, indicate that the accretion columns in these two components are likely geometrically similar.  Additionally, PX 1555-43 displays an unusually high mass accretion rate.  Asynchronous polars show evidence of magnetic reconnection heating contributing to their X-ray emission, and PX 1555-43's spectrum suggests an increased contribution from this reconnection.  Spectra from the Chandra and XMM-Newton for HH 332-1 and HH 332-2 show some discrepancy in their parameters, which may be attributed to an instrumental bias.  Further study is needed to confirm this finding.

We have developed an efficient and robust partitioned method for solving fluid-structure interaction (FSI) problems. Our approach involves separating the solution processes for the fluid and solid domains, with a two-step method comprising a nonlinear Newton-Raphson scheme for the solid and a semi-implicit method for the fluid. We have investigated the stability of this scheme and established a condition on the time step that ensures stability. Our approach has been implemented using a finite element method for the fluid and a finite element or boundary element method for the solid. Our results show that our approach can provide accurate solutions for various FSI problems, including those involving flexible structures and dynamic loading conditions.

We introduce HiTMap, a novel mapping framework that leverages a local metric approach for autonomous navigation in complex and dynamic indoor environments. Unlike conventional global metric maps, HiTMap partitions the space into locally manageable areas, using partially ordered metric spaces to avoid dealing with topological implications. We demonstrate the efficacy of HiTMap by adapting the commonly used iLQG optimization approach, utilizing a sampling method for real-world implementation. Our method's effectiveness is demonstrated through indoor navigation simulations and subsequent testing on a real robotic platform in a dynamic environment, showing that HiTMap-based navigation can be a viable approach.

We designed and tested a series of models to identify toxic behavior in Twitter posts, using a previously established dataset.  Our best model, which we believed to be quite simple, consisted of a RoBERTa-based classifier that leveraged supervised learning techniques.  This model was particularly impressive, as it demonstrated a strong ability to detect abusive content with a macro F1 score of 0.8976, which represented a significant improvement over previous attempts using similar techniques.  Our analysis of the results revealed that the model exhibited both high precision and recall rates, which are essential qualities for systems aimed at preventing the spread of hate speech and other forms of toxic behavior on social media platforms.

Researchers used atomic interferometry to test a hypothetical local magnetic field at the atomic scale and found it could detect fields as weak as 10^-20 Tesla meters^-1 over a distance of one atomic diameter. To achieve this level of sensitivity, measurements were taken in a vacuum environment with minimal influence from light. The method involves observing the variation in CO2 molecule isomers due to interactions with a local magnetic field and subsequent exposure to coherent light. The sensitivity in this test exceeded previous limitations by a thousand times. Researchers found that the most sensitive detection point occurred at one atomic diameter and demonstrated agreement between theoretical local field responses and experimental data. The level of sensitivity achieved indicates that atomic interferometry can detect local magnetic field influences on atomic and molecular scale reactions.

Our research introduces an innovative concept of a magnetic heterostructure based on EuO/EuS(001) binary compounds, which enables the magnetocaloric effect to be selectively tuned for either spin-up or spin-down electrons through spatial composition variation. Using Auger current spectroscopy and scanning tunneling microscopy, we measured a notable difference in cooling power for spin-up and spin-down electrons at the EuO/EuS interface, which exhibits opposite symmetry compared to both EuO and EuS separately. The calculated results demonstrate that changing the electron spin can alter the spatial composition of the EuO/EuS heterostructure, thereby modifying the magnitude of the change in entropy and ultimately the magnetocaloric effect. Notably, this phenomenon allows us to design the cooling power for a specific spin orientation, thereby enabling the development of spin-dependent thermal devices.

We introduce a novel method for calculating light dispersion within a semiconductor lattice, where we treat the gap width as an effective, spatially varying quantity. This approach surpasses local models by accurately capturing light behavior near defects. Using a modified Dyson equation, we quantify the impact of disorder on light dispersion within the gap, obtaining reliable results through numerical simulations. In addition, we demonstrate that our effective gap model can be applied to analyze light propagation within fractal structures, and we compare our method to existing local models.

The calculus of constructions was a groundbreaking construct for various contemporary programming languages and type theories. Introduced over three decades ago, it has significantly impacted the development of many influential ideas in programming languages and type theory. This collection of advanced type-theoretic concepts, which incorporates functional and dependent types, has inspired numerous notable languages and frameworks such as Coq, Agda, and Idris. This survey presents an in-depth analysis of how the calculus of constructions has evolved since its inception and explores the various ways its core principles have been applied across different programming languages and environments.

The increasing popularity of the entanglement concept in quantum electronics research necessitates a clear and straightforward explanation of entanglement properties.
This article demonstrates the utility of basic quantum mechanics principles, utilizing both the correlator method and the von-Neumann density-matrix approach, to derive straightforward formulas for calculating entanglement characteristics in various diode configurations, including the DC-biased double-barrier resonant-tunneling diode and the DC-biased Gunn diode.

In a Bayesian setting, assigning a Dirichlet process prior to densities results in the incorporation of a significant amount of information into the model, which in turn leads to the non-identifiable recovery of admixture weights. To address this issue, a variation of the progressive cures was placed on the densities, ensuring that the weights are retrievable in an almost sure and unique manner. Furthermore, this modified model was shown to be asymptotically equivalent to the standard Dirichlet process mixture model with the added benefit of coherent posterior samples. To facilitate practical application, a representation of the progressive cure Dirichlet process through stick-breaking was also established, enabling the utilization of recent results on the consistency of the slope estimates in general contexts. Additionally, theoretical evidence was presented to support the notion that the weights' identifiability is a direct result of the cure parameter's influence on the sample weights, resulting in the formulation of a new method that retrieves these weights with enhanced accuracy. Results from simulated data and a real-life cancer diagnosis dataset demonstrated the superiority of the proposed method over conventional approaches.

A calculation of two-loop corrections to the anomalous dimensions of twist-four operators in N=4 SYM theory using the BFKL lattice is presented. A correction of one order in the expansion is quantified, allowing for a comparison with the BFKL approach through the dispersion relation. This leads to an implicit understanding of two-loop anomalous dimensions through the BFKL kernel, specifically its impact on the BPS shockwave vertex when considering interactions between BPS strings in six-dimensional type IIB supergravity. Additionally, this calculation demonstrates the compatibility of the BFKL lattice with the BFKL dispersion relation, yielding a correction of one order for the anomalous dimension of one of the twist-four operators and providing an upper limit for the correction of the remaining operators.

We introduce DynaSOAr, a cutting-edge GPU memory allocator that leverages streaming partitions and sort-merge algorithms to expedite memory reclamation through conflict resolution. Unlike conventional GPU allocators, DynaSOAr enhances performance and lessens memory fragmentation by concurrently managing GPU memory. In our evaluation, DynaSOAr demonstrates superior performance and reduced fragmentation when compared to both a basic stochastic allocator and TBS, a leading sorting-based allocator. Specifically, DynaSOAr accelerates memory reclamation by a factor of at least two to five times, achieves up to 4x lower fragmentation, and accelerates various GPU application workloads by 1.5x to 7x.

This research paper investigates the boundedness and continuity of operators generated by singular integral operators, when applied to functions within certain complex space domains known as mixed Morrey spaces. Building on previous findings, our study expands on its assumptions and successfully achieves the desired outcomes in a broader range of operator types and space domains. Additionally, related sub-operators and their continuity within certain complex space domains are also explored in this research.

Our calculations show that YSR states near ferromagnetic adatoms or dimers undergo a significant shift due to spin-orbit coupling, contradicting the common assumption of their independence from spin. Using a 2D tight-binding model, we demonstrate how SOC affects YSR states and their mapping to the local magnetization, and reveal that its impact is particularly pronounced for flat YSR states near the Fermi level. Furthermore, we find that the orientation of adatoms or dimers has a substantial influence on their YSR state spectra, with a clear shift in energy that can be as large as 10 meV, depending on the direction and separation between the spin-orbit ions. With superconducting proximity mapping considered, we predict that the apparent magnetization near these atoms or pairs could change from a low-value minimum to a high-value maximum or minimum, with a distinct preference for flat YSR states that can be adjusted through tension in the YZ plane.

FourierMask est une méthode de segmentation par maskes avancée qui utilise des fonctions implicites pour créer des masques à résolution accrue à partir d'images en résolution fixe. FourierMask est une approche innovante qui utilise des rérepresentations spectrales pour modéliser les relations entre les images et les masques, permettant une gestion flexible des variables de placement de base. En utilisant l'apprentissage automatique pour ajuster des coefficients spectraux, FourierMask peut générer des masques précis à résolution accrue sans recourir à la déformation de la grille de grille. En comparant FourierMask avec des méthodes de segmentation par maskes plus traditionnelles, nous constatons que FourierMask atteint des performances équivalentes ou supérieures dans huit domaines, atteignant une précision de 0,94 pour la segmentation des formes et une précision de 0,95 pour la segmentation des personnages. Le code et les modèles sont disponibles sur GitHub, tandis que les résultats sont accessible sur AirTable.

We provide specific examples of minimal disks in three-dimensional space that are completely filled and have finite area, contradicting the long-held conjecture that such disks are flat. Additionally, we demonstrate that every submanifold with a non-negative curvature in three-dimensional space has a limited number of disks similar to those described above.

The feature known as cloud veiling, where an core cloud is obscured by surrounding clouds and alters the observed shape, has been a recognized phenomenon for cloud analysis, albeit with a more conventional visual assessment. However, with the advancement of cloud detection technology using shape theory, this veiling effect poses significant challenges to understanding cloud structure from satellite images. Based on mathematical theories of shape detection and veiling effects, this study proposes an approach to recovering the core of clouds from their surrounding clouds. Specifically, it is hypothesized that the core of a cloud, which is shaped by wind forces, can be represented as the Minkowski sum of its boundary and a line segment representing veiled portions. Building on previous work, this study formulates a method to estimate the core's dimensions and distance from its boundary through the application of beta shape theory. Experimental results with real satellite images demonstrate that this approach is both feasible and effective in recovering the core clouds.

The complex interaction between a chirped laser pulse and two-layer targets composed of a thin, low-density secondary layer surrounding a higher-density core is investigated through a series of particle-in-cell simulations. The findings show that in cases where the critical density layer corresponds to the secondary target layer, significant acceleration of ions occurs, achieving multiple times the laser speed. A detailed analysis reveals that an enigmatic enhancement in ion acceleration discovered in earlier research is, in fact, a result of an electron void that forms above the target, incorporating parts of the laser pulse and the accelerated ions. A key condition for this electron void to persist is met when the laser's depletions move at a speed equal to half its group velocity, which is shown to occur when the critical density layer is located within the laser pulse's area of influence. As a result, ions are accelerated within an electrostatic field that forms within the electron void and encompassing the surviving electrons. Additionally, it is demonstrated that increasing the degree of laser chirping can enhance ion acceleration, while also complicating the formation of the electron void due to increased electron motion across the target, but that a specific optimal level of chirping exists that balances these factors for maximum ion acceleration.

A pair of transiting mini-Neptunes have been discovered orbiting the G5V star KOI-423, which is roughly 320 parsecs from the Sun. These planets fall within the habitable zone's broad extension and surround the star at an almost 90-degree angle. Our research suggests the planets have sizes of about 4.54 to 4.83 times the radius of the Earth, with the former likely being the more accurate measurement. Their masses were estimated to be around 25 to 43 times the mass of the Earth. Our team's analysis indicates the planets likely maintain stable and long-term orbits, and both planets exhibit similar densities, with values of about 0.34 to 0.51 grams per cubic centimeter. Given their placement in the habitable zone and suitable orbit, these planets present promising candidates for hosting conditions suitable for life.

We used a combination of computational modeling and experimental analysis to understand the behavior of carbon and nitrogen in rutile TiO2. By incorporating these elements in interstitial and substitutional forms, we found significant variations in their behavior. In interstitial positions, C and N displayed a strong tendency to occupy the [O] hole and formed anion-like and cathion-like states respectively. In contrast, substitutional C and N took on a more neutral character and had smaller binding energies when compared to their interstitial counterparts. XPS and EPR measurements confirmed our theoretical findings and offered further insight into the properties of C and N in TiO2. Our study also revealed that these defects act as suitable candidates for optical and electrical modulation in TiO2-based devices.

The ATLAS experiment at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC) has investigated flavor-changing neutral current decays of the top quark using a semi-elastic process with an analyzing power. The process in question involves a top quark produced in association with a heavy flavor jet, for which the flavor of the jet can be determined by analyzing the charge asymmetry distribution in semi-elastic decays of the top quark. With an integrated luminosity of 3 inverse femtobarns of proton-proton collisions at a center-of-mass energy of 13 TeV, the analysis finds that the branching ratio limits for $t\rightarrow u\gamma$ and $t\rightarrow c\gamma$ decays are $B(t\rightarrow u\gamma)<5.8\times10^{-6}$ and $B(t\rightarrow c\gamma)<2.5\times10^{-5}$ at 95% confidence level. Additionally, the analysis places an upper limit on the branching ratio of the $t\rightarrow uZ$ decay at $B(t\rightarrow uZ)<1.0\times10^{-4}$ for a gauge boson with a mass range of 50-900 GeV.

The X-ray Integral Field Unit (X-IFU) on the Athena telescope will significantly contribute to the study of intra-cluster medium turbulence. X-IFU's spatially-integrated X-ray spectroscopy is optimized to map turbulence and its connection with thermal energy in galaxy clusters through its impact on X-ray emission spectra. Understanding turbulence's role in maintaining cluster thermal balance is crucial, to then use this knowledge to constrain turbulence models and thus improve measurements of mass distributions within clusters through X-ray emission mapping. X-IFU's measurements will also inform scientists about the cluster's cooling state and gas distribution, and its observations will likely reveal turbulence's connection with gas accretion, star formation, and gas entropy in clusters for the first time.

We explored the minimum number of colors required to color the edges of a given graph G around a subgraph F, allowing for the possibility of monochromatic edges. This edge-coloring problem has been investigated for various types of graph F, including a triangle, which is the focus of our initial inquiry. We established a specific lower bound for the number of colors needed when F is a triangle and demonstrated that this lower bound can be achieved through a specific construction. This construction was not previously described in the literature. Additionally, if F contains at least two triangles that do not share any vertices, we proved that the minimum number of colors required is at least |F| + 1. These results expand our understanding of the edge-coloring problems and verify previously known lower bounds for certain types of graph F.

Observations of 13CO in the Central Molecular Zone (CMZ) of our galaxy using the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA) reveal a distinct density pattern within this region. While the density distribution becomes more irregular at smaller scales, it exhibits a linear anisotropy similar to 1.5 when considering larger scales. A linear anisotropy lower than anisotropy at larger scales is also observed in the Bar and the Spiral Arm adjacent to the CMZ. A comparative study between these regions suggests that the unique linear anisotropy in the CMZ may be a feature present on a scale similar to 100 parsecs, where it starts to disappear as smaller-scale structures become apparent. A possible explanation for this linear anisotropy is a gravitational potential with a bar or quadripole component, where it could be a clue for identifying gas reserves within 500 parsecs of the galaxy's center.

Most current face-detection techniques are complicated by unnecessary information and hindered by code smells. This paper introduces a simple eye-detection system that leverages eye-focused defaults, eliminating the need for face-code and subsequent facial-feature-code. By doing so, significant improvements in model compactness and speed are achieved. The eye-detection system utilizes a minimalistic design, incorporating eye-focused default rules to decrease parameters and layers, thereby enhancing overall performance. The paper also presents EyeFinder, an eye-detection model that showcases enhanced efficiency and model compactness when applied to the MEFAC dataset. The eye-detection system demonstrates the potential for improved face-detection accuracy through a systematic approach, encompassing both methodological and systematic assessments.

Our investigation reveals that qutrits demonstrate greater endurance in mass measurement, particularly when subjected to depolarizing or stabilizer noise, as indicated by our simulations utilizing error-affected qutrit and qubit circuits. Furthermore, our analysis across various noise levels uncovers distinct threshold behaviors in error propagation, which can be understood through a novel, exact analysis in the single-qutrit case. This new comprehension also enables the derivation of an overall error bound in the qutrit scenario, which yields a notably more favorable exponential growth in measurement accuracy compared to the qubit case. Consequently, our findings validate the initial intuition that larger-dimensional systems can provide improved resistance to measurement error. In addition, our research introduces a general framework for describing the trade-off between system dimensionality and error tolerance in measurement determination.

To achieve our goal of producing highly polarized positrons with more than 30% polarization for potential use in next-generation colliders or experiments, we have designed and built an innovative scheme for polarizing positrons through Bremsstrahlung radiation while in flight. This system involves the generation of a strong magnetic field that surrounds a lengthened section of the storage ring, where a beam of polarized positrons passes through a mid-air Bremsstrahlung radiation interaction with an X-ray target. Due to the challenge of creating a strong magnetic field over a lengthy area, we decided to utilize a novel approach using a hollow magnetic cylinder to increase the magnetic field inside by up to three-fold compared to an ordinary cylindrical design. Through computational simulations, we were able to determine that this novel cylinder design can effectively enhance the polarization of positrons to over 30% through Bremsstrahlung radiation. Moreover, our research revealed that this scheme has sufficient tolerance to accommodate variations in beam current, potential magnetic field deviations, and possible changes in Bremsstrahlung radiation characteristics. Finally, we were able to estimate that this system could effectively produce highly polarized positrons with more than 30% polarization at a rate of up to 0.25 electrons (positrons) per second.

In this paper, we explore the polynomial diameter concept in finite groups, specifically convergent series representing the diameter for a substantial class of groups, including those with few conjugacy classes and nilpotent subgroups. Building on the work of Gilmer and others, we demonstrate that various groups with the property of $\pi$-number for a specific prime set $\pi$ possess polynomial diameter, further showcasing that groups whose conjugacy classes are parameterized by irreducible polynomials over $\mathbb{F}_p$ have polynomial diameter. Additionally, we establish that for any given prime $p$, the vast majority of groups in the family $p\mathcal{K}$ exhibit polynomial diameter, fueled by the observation that most groups in this family have a super-infinite number of conjugacy classes.

A temperature can be determined using a single sensor that measures the resistance in a binary counter circuit. The counter's resolution and inaccuracy are addressed by modifying its structure. The invention of a temperature sensor that relies on the 1/K relationship between temperature and resistance is described. This sensor works with any type of resistor, whether it's carbon, metal, or semiconductor, and it maintains a high accuracy of 0.1 degrees Celsius for a wide temperature range of -20 to 120 degrees Celsius. The sensor's cost is low, it has a high reliability, and it can be used in various applications, such as medical equipment, cars, and military technology.

The ideal magnetohydrodynamic beta limit in toroidal stars has been found to increase with the strength of the magnetic field when the toroidal and poloidal components are interlinked. This effect only holds when the stars have sufficient mass to prevent the displacement of mass across their surface. The interaction between the toroidal and poloidal components plays a crucial role in determining the stability of magnetic field configurations in stars. The influence of rotation on these components affects the stability in a way that is contrary to what is observed in tokamaks. In tokamaks, the rotation of plasma has the effect of increasing the ideal magnetohydrodynamic beta limit by reducing the magnitude of the interlinked component. The rotation of stars has the opposite effect, causing the ideal magnetohydrodynamic beta limit to decrease. The relationship between rotation and the limit remains unchanged when the stars have sufficient mass to prevent the displacement of mass across their surface. The findings of this study suggest that the rotation of stars, like the rotation of plasma in solar prominences and filaments, is capable of maintaining their stability. The discovery of rapid stellar rotations in a significant number of low mass stars, together with the fact that the rotation of stars can produce substantial stresses on their surfaces, implies that stellar rotations can shape the stars' magnetic field configurations in a way that are similar to what is observed in solar prominences and filaments. The stresses generated by rotation can potentially lead to the formation of stable stellar flux tubes in the outer layers of tor

Our investigation proposes a novel approach to explaining the irreversibility of renormalization group flows via an analogy with fluid dynamics. According to this analogy, the RG equation represents a fluid flow influenced by an external force, where the RG time is akin to the fluid's velocity, and the scaling operator two-point functions are linked to the fluid's resistance and capacity in the same way that viscosity and heat capacity are in standard thermofluid dynamics. Utilizing this analogy, we interpret the irreversibility of the RG flow as entropy production resulting from the work done against the fluid's flow by its own force, a concept that is mathematically validated through the use of Bogoliubov's Bogoliubov functional integral representation. Our proposed framework also successfully connects the difference between RG equations in the bulk and near a boundary to the entropy gradient in the same way that the heat capacity of a boundary in thermofluid dynamics accounts for the heat stored within the boundary, leading to new insights into the phenomenon of boundary fine tuning. Moreover, our proposed framework provides an interpretation of the Lagrangian density as the free energy density of the system, and links the irreversibility of the RG flow to the non-coincidence of the Lagrangian and action densities, resulting in a new expression for the entropy production during the RG flow in terms of the imaginary part of the on-shell two-point function of the stress tensor.

Music listeners frequently search for lyrics and song audio to enhance their listening experience, but conventional web search engines aren't optimized for music searches due to the text-based nature of search queries. In contrast, our proposed search engine, AudioSearch, allows users to search for audio by speaking or singing a snippet of a song they're listening to. Unlike conventional search engines that return vast amounts of text data, AudioSearch yields relevant audio results, consisting of song excerpts, in response to user queries. In our experimentation phase, we gathered a substantial dataset of user-generated data, comprising over 1,800 search queries and corresponding audio responses, but unfortunately, it wasn't suitable for formal evaluation due to data quality issues. Nevertheless, our preliminary findings indicate that classifying music searches according to their intent (identifying songs, searching for lyrics, looking for related artists, or exploring genres) is a complex task due to the gray areas that exist between these categories.

Research on topological groupoids was initially met with skepticism by some experts in the field. Despite this, the idea has found applications in the study of topological stacks and higher stacks in the realm of algebraic geometry. The paper at hand develops the concept of a topological groupoid extension, which is used to create a connection between topological groupoids and higher stacks. The authors demonstrate that topological groupoids can be utilized as representations of gerbes over topological stacks, obtained through descent theory. The paper also explores the relationship between morphisms in this representation and the objects in the gerbe, which leads to an understanding of the Picard group of a topological stack through the representation of the classifying stack of the Picard groupoid. The authors further establish that this representation is essentially surjective, which provides a topological groupoid-based description of the cohomology class of a line bundle over a stack. The paper concludes with the discussion of its findings in the context of recent research.

Our research focuses on the relationship between molecular core mass and the formation of massive stars. It is crucial to monitor core mass evolution to understand the self-regulation of massive star formation. By utilizing millimeter interferometry with the Atacama Large Millimeter/submillimeter Array (ALMA), we studied the mass growth of 12 massive molecular cores in the 20 $\mu$m source fields within the Milky Way. These cores were selected based on their large sizes and high densities. Our ALMA observations allowed us to detect H$_2$S(1,1) emission, which indicated the presence of high-mass star formation, and enabled us to estimate core masses using a formula related to the velocity gradient. We found that four cores with detected water masers showed a significant increase in mass, with one reaching a mass of approximately 1000 $M_{\odot}$. Three of these four cores are now hosting ethynyl maser sources, which are known to be indicators of the formation of massive stars. We also observed that the mass growth rates in our sample exceed 100 $M_{\odot}$ yr$^{-1}$, which are comparable to values found for some galactic giant starless cores. Our findings suggest that molecular core mass growth can reach extremely high rates under specific conditions, further supporting the concept that massive star formation is self-regulated due to radiation-driven gas outflows, which limit core mass growth.

Our proof demonstrates that the class of finite Godel algebras, which are essentially forest-like in structure, is equivalent to the class of finite Boolean algebras with operators that are derived from BAO with the operator domain being a forest, and this equivalence is based on a natural dual connection between these two classes.

In 3D LiDAR-based classification tasks, local features extracted from individual points are usually independent of neighboring points. This study challenges that approach by investigating the impact of surrounding context on classification performance. We introduce a novel method known as Context Extraction Transformer (CET) that leverages nearby information from LiDAR data to enhance classification capabilities. In CET, a context extraction module is incorporated into the transformer encoder to aggregate neighboring point data from multiple sensors. CET is evaluated through real-world experiments conducted in agricultural and forest environments, utilizing K-fold cross-validation to assess its effectiveness. Compared to conventional methods, CET demonstrates superior classification performance across various sensors, achieving accuracy rates of +6.4% and +4.8% in agricultural and forest scenarios, respectively. Additionally, CET exhibits greater robustness to point density variations.

Classical operations of differentiation and integration applied to a well-known class of functions, which remain unchanged under any coordinate rotation, yield results that no longer preserve this property unless certain conditions are met. The conditions required for positivity definiteness of these operations are established and shown to be equivalent to sufficient conditions related to the eigenvalues of a specific matrix. Furthermore, this study sheds light on the limitations of using approximate methods, such as Gaussian integration, to accurately represent these functions, especially in relation to their spectral interpolation properties.

The discovery of a possible connection between ultra-high-energy cosmic rays and neutrinos has been an open question for a long time. While it remains unclear whether cosmic rays can cause neutrino events, we have observed in our previous study a possible link between neutrino events and cosmic rays within the energy range of $E_{\textrm{neu}}\ge10^{18.5}$ eV, where an alleged correlation exists. In this paper, we update that finding with a larger data set from eight years of BAMBA neutrino data and sixty-six years of Telescope Array cosmic ray data. By calculating the Poisson disk grid radius as one-neighth of the neutron radius, we updated the radius to 788 km in neutrino data and 1075 km in cosmic ray data. With this new radius, we found eight new events within the energy range of $E_{\textrm{neu}}\ge10^{19}$ eV, where seven of those events share a connection with cosmic rays. This result raises the total number of possible neutrino-cosmic ray connections to fifteen within the energy range of $E_{\textrm{neu}}\ge10^{18.5}$ eV. Additionally, we found three new events within the energy range of $E_{\textrm{neu}}\ge10^{19.5}$ eV, where two of those events share a connection with cosmic rays. This result raises

Theoretical models explaining the flow of liquid foams through narrow channels often incorporate a roughness factor that accounts for how the surface roughness of the channel affects the foam's viscosity. Determining this factor, however, has been a challenge for researchers. Our research offers a way to measure the roughness factor by observing how the surface of the foam changes as it flows and undergoes collisions, providing a more comprehensive understanding of its behavior and potentially leading to new ways of studying foam dynamics.

Ensemble-based Convolutional Neural Networks (CNN) have reached remarkable performance in image classification tasks. Combining multiple CNNs through ensemble classification yields superior results above using a single, optimized CNN. Our research delves into ensemble classification versus the optimization of a solo CNN through systematic evaluations. We conducted exhaustive experiments utilizing 12 diverse datasets across three categories - animal sounds, food items, and general object recognition - comprising 4 interior datasets (MNIST, Fashion, Vehicle, and Digits) and 8 exterior datasets (CIFAR, Places, Stanford, and MS). Each dataset was subjected to exhaustive parameter tuning for both ensemble classification and solo CNN optimization. The results consistently showed ensemble classification outperforming solo CNN optimization, with an average improvement of 5.4% across all datasets. Notably, this advantage was particularly pronounced in datasets with low training sizes, demonstrating ensemble classification's potential for handling data scarcity.

The interplay of surface tension and rotational force shapes the anisotropic viscosity of a rotating Hele-Shaw cell, influencing the stability of various states, from linear to circular patterns, and how they transition at a critical rotation rate. Adjusting the surface tension through membrane tension modifies the anisotropic viscosity coefficients, affecting the stability of these states. Using high-resolution imaging, we observe and record the precise sequences of states in a rotating Hele-Shaw cell with anisotropic viscosity, discovering new patterns, such as the formation of lines and zig-zag shapes, and establishing a new regime for the instability of linear patterns. Our study also introduces a new method to study anisotropic fluids by recreating the same dynamics using rotating membranes. We analyze and explain our findings using both laboratory and theoretically-derived data.

We examine the average work done by a many-body system in contact with an heat bath, using the quantum Langevin equation to study a quantum many-body system and define an equation for average work that reflects the internal interactions of the system. By dividing the system into two parts, we demonstrate that the work done can be attributed to a thermal part and an internal part that follows the pattern of microwork first proposed by Martinovici. Additionally, we derive an expression for the change in microwork that incorporates time-correlation functions and apply this understanding to study a quantum spin system composed of Heisenberg spins.

Our study reveals variations in the relative abundances of CCH and CN radicals within jet-cooled cyclopentadiene and benzene. By utilizing the INTRUDER program to compute potential energy curves and nonadiabatic interactions, we determined relative energies and levels of mixing between the $\pi$-bonded X$^2$$\Pi$ and the $\sigma$-bonded X$^2$$\Sigma$ states for both molecules. In contrast to benzene, where the X$^2$$\Pi$ state is more than 5.0 kJ/mol higher in energy than the X$^2$$\Sigma$ state, we found the X$^2$$\Pi$ state to be only about 1.5 kJ/mol more energetic in cyclopentadiene. As a result, the relative abundance of CCH compared to CN within cyclopentadiene is nearly four times greater than within benzene. By comparing results from ab initio computations and experimental data, we were also able to determine the extent of electronic mixing, or vibron nonlinearity, within these molecules, with an estimated 20% of vibronic character in the X$^2$$\Pi$ state and 5% in the X$^2$$\Sigma$ state.

The attention mechanism in neural machine translation has been the subject of significant study in recent years. To further improve translation accuracy, this paper introduces a look-ahead attention model that incorporates information from future elements in the input sentence. We propose an iterative attention model that simultaneously considers both previous and future contexts. To mitigate the negative impact of noisy information from future elements, a reliability-based model that integrates previous and current attention scores is also explored. Experimental results on the WMT English-to-German and Spanish-to-English translation tasks demonstrate the effectiveness of our proposed models in improving translation accuracy.

The Grids and Clouds (G&C) research community has adopted a translational approach, closely collaborating with industry and other stakeholders to effectively address practical problems and showcase the feasibility of G&C technologies. This approach has led to significant advancements and notable successes, including innovative solutions and notable infrastructure developments. However, there is concern that the community's advances may be outrunning its underlying foundations, given the significant scientific challenges and open issues in areas such as resource management, scheduling, and performance evaluation. This concern is further compounded by the need for more robust security measures and better support for new computing paradigms like Big Data and Cloud computing. This report provides an objective analysis of the current state of G&C research, highlighting both the remarkable progress made and the outstanding challenges that remain to be addressed in this field.

We've established a cosmological monodromy model with a universal viscous fluid, which leads to the formation of five additional e-folds of inflationary periods. The model demonstrates how an almost flat universe can evolve from an initially curved state, and through the process of cosmic inflation, it becomes exponentially expanded and smoothed. The likely explanation for the universe's current almost flat state is the visitations of the universe to a series of 'branes with high tension', which occur during the inflationary periods. The universe then experiences a gradual cooling following these periods, and we find that the viscosity coefficient has a significant influence on this process, though it ultimately plays a lesser role in the overall expansion of the universe. The findings also indicate that the universe's temperature during the inflationary periods was too extremely low for the existence of particles, and that the universe's curvature is continually decreasing over time due to the ongoing effects of the viscous fluid.

Recent studies have demonstrated that peer influences are a key driver of curiosity, with our research expanding on these findings by examining their impact on curiosity within a collaborative learning environment. We have been tasked with exploring the relationship between curiosity and peer interactions to gain insights on the following queries: Do individuals with higher curiosity tend to be drawn into productive discussions with their peers or get sidetracked by unessential topics? Do learners who are more curious benefit from being placed in groups with peers who have similar or differing levels of curiosity? Our results from a simulated collaborative learning activity involving 81 participants revealed the following outcomes: individuals with higher curiosity were more likely to engage in fulfilling interactions with their peers, were less prone to getting distracted in group settings, and fared better when paired with peers who have similar levels of curiosity. These findings were confirmed through both quantitative and qualitative analysis. Moreover, we have established a condition under which cooperative learning can lead to an increase in curiosity, and are presenting initial ideas on representing the relationships between curiosity, peer interactions, and group dynamics through a formal model.

We introduce a Python 2.7 and 3.5 implementation for graph-based Matérn Gaussian processes which seamlessly adapts to both mini-batch and non-conjugate settings through the use of black box variational inference. This code provides an efficient way to deploy these models, making them easily accessible for the research community to build upon. Additionally, our work is relevant to several prominent research areas including deep probabilistic flows, graph signal processing, and time series forecasting, and is particularly suited for complex data sets found in areas such as neuroscience and social network analyses. The implementation, research tools, and example use cases are available at https://github/matern-graph.

In monitoring and responding to changes in urban road networks, researchers often utilize graph theory and signal processing to optimize information coverage and reliability. While previous studies have investigated the benefits of incorporating mobile sensors into wireless sensor networks, the potential of ridesourcing vehicles, which can navigate and sense any part of the network, has not been thoroughly explored. This paper proposes a method to determine the optimal distribution of ridesourcing vehicles within a network by solving a coverage and reliability problem, and demonstrates the approach using a transportation network in the state of Michigan. Furthermore, the proposed algorithm is evaluated under various conditions and compared with alternative methods.

Utilizing a total of $13.6$ picobarns of data collected at the $\tau$-lepton threshold and $7.0$ picobarns above it, as well as $7.0$ picobarns of data collected at the $J/	au 	o$ threshold, researchers were able to establish an upper limit on the $J/	au 	o 	ext{invisible}$ branching fraction of $4.1	au 10^{-4}$ at a $95\%$ confidence level. Additionally, they set an upper limit on the dark matter-nucleon scattering cross section of $3.8	au 10^{-41}$ $	au 	au 	(m_\tau^2)$ $	au 	2.5	au 10^{-41}$ $	au 	au 	(m_\tau^2+1)$ $	au 	au 	(1	m_\tau^2)$ cm$^2$ at a $95\%$ confidence level, establishing this as the most stringent limit to date.

We introduce a variable stepsize stochastic general linear model (SGLM) that utilizes information from nonuniformly spaced data points, in contrast to traditional variable stepsize SGLMs which assume equally spaced observations. Our model shares similarities with Gaussian process signal models, but with a linear representation. We demonstrate that the minimum mean squared error (MMSE) estimate from our variable stepsize SGLM can be computed efficiently through a linear algebraic approach, which is then extended to develop a simple and effective method for MMSE estimation on dense grids. Our variable stepsize SGLM is particularly beneficial for scenarios where computing resources are limited and the grid density needs to be adjusted dynamically in response to changing environmental conditions, resulting in significant reductions in the required number of grid points in certain scenarios. Our research is relevant to the broader community as it provides a variable stepsize SGLM solution that can be incorporated into bayesian filtering algorithms, such as the Gaussian mixture SGLM. Our approach is also adaptable to settings with delayed or missing observations, which is essential for the development of robust bayesian filtering algorithms that incorporate online learning.

MFSSA offers a groundbreaking approach to handling complex signal sequences, but its practical application has been limited so far, likely due to the absence of an efficient optimization method. The lack of a suitable algorithm has forced researchers to rely on suboptimal solutions, thereby hindering the full potential of MFSSA. To bridge this gap, we introduce a cutting-edge tensor-tri-factorization-based algorithm to solve the MFSSA problem explicitly. The new method leverages both the advantages of tensor decomposition and alternating direction methods for constrained optimization to tackle the challenge. The resulting system allows for the direct solution of the MFSSA problem, enabling the extraction of signal features from sequences with varying lengths. To evaluate its performance, the new algorithm was tested on synthetic data, curves representing temperature dynamics, and remote sensing images, demonstrating its superior accuracy compared to traditional low-rank factorization methods. Furthermore, the algorithm exhibits scalability, as evidenced by its ability to handle over 1 million data points.

Recent deep learning models have successfully applied neural networks to automate tasks like math problem-solving and image classification, and they have also shown potential in automatically scoring written content, such as essays. Nonetheless, research has revealed that these models can exhibit flawed behaviors when scoring certain types of content. In particular, some models display over-sensitivity and over-stability in their evaluations, where even minor changes in the input result in significant score variations. In this research, we will explore the implications of these models on educational assessments and investigate methods for enhancing their robustness and reliability. In order to achieve this goal, we will propose evaluation criteria for automatic essay scoring models that can detect over-sensitivity and over-stability. Additionally, we will develop novel techniques for boosting the robustness and reliability of these models. Our research utilizes a combination of both data-driven and model-based approaches. Firstly, we will implement stress tests to assess the models' performance in complex scenarios and evaluate their reliability. Secondly, we will employ techniques such as adversarial training and data augmentation to enhance the models' robustness. Our research will focus on evaluating the Munich University Language Model, a popular deep learning model, and will explore its applications in scoring educational assessments. Our findings demonstrate that the models' evaluations correlate with human evaluators' feedback, and that enhancing the models' performance improves their ability to accurately assess the quality of written content, particularly in complex scenarios. In conclusion, our research provides valuable insights into the behaviors of deep learning models and proposes methods

This research examines the asymptotic behavior of a random walk whose step sizes have an average of zero and are independent of one another. The long-term distribution of the random walk's position can be influenced by a parameter 'b' which represents the spectral radius of a matrix whose off-diagonal elements are 1 and whose diagonal elements are a series of positive values that add up to a number less than two. If 'b' is less than one, the random walk's distribution will eventually behave like a normal distribution with mean zero and a variance that is equal to the sum of the square of each individual variance that makes up the matrix 'b'. If 'b' is greater than one but has a long-term average of zero, the random walk's distribution will eventually behave like a normal distribution weighted by the likelihood of each individual variance as it makes up the matrix 'b'. If 'b' is equal to one, the random walk's distribution will behave like a rotated Cauchy distribution. If the variance of each individual step is equal to one, the random walk's distribution will behave like a rotated Cauchy distribution with a scale of sqrt(2*π) multiplied by the likelihood of each individual variance as it makes up the matrix 'b'.
